title: The Pass Is Closed
hook: Ninety minutes of mountain you can't have yet.
scene: Spokane is two hundred and eighty miles east, and the only road that gets there climbs a pass you can't take on a permit, can't take alone, and can't take until you're better than you are right now. Gracie's on the passenger seat with her paws tucked. Mya's beside her, taking up more room than she needs to. They came because they always come. So today you do the small version: you go get the license, and then you start being someone who can drive the pass.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: State the goal in miles. The pass is closed. Both cats are with her. Today is the license.

title: Before the Engine
hook: The key's in your hand. You haven't turned it.
scene: The lot's wet and empty and the car has been sitting since yesterday, which is long enough for a lot of small things to change without asking you. Gracie and Mya are already on the seat. The key's in your hand.
decision: Before you start it, what do you do?

options.text: Turn the key. You already know this car.
options.result: It catches on the first try, the way it always does. You pull out on everything you knew yesterday. The car sat all night in a lot that didn't stay the same shape while it did.

options.text: Get out and walk it, all the way around
options.result: Tires. Glass. Nothing behind the bumper, nothing under it. Both doors shut the way you left them. It takes forty seconds and then the key means something.

options.text: Check your phone, then start it
options.result: You read the screen. The screen doesn't know anything about the ground around your wheels, and now you've spent the only time you were going to give this.

options.text: Open the door, sit back down, start it
options.result: You get half out, look at nothing in particular, and sit down again. The engine starts on the same view you already had.

debrief: Walk the car before you start it — tires, glass, and the ground around the wheels.

source.psdp_skill: Skill one: before you start the engine
source.teaching_target: Before the engine. Walk the car once. Do not start from memory.

title: The Belt
hook: Your belt's in your hand. Neither cat is.
scene: They ride loose. They've always ridden loose, and there's no version of these two where that changes, so the question isn't what to do about them. It's what to do about you.
decision: Before you move, what do you fasten?

options.text: Nothing. It's a parking lot.
options.result: You leave it hanging. Then something moves in the lot and you're not attached to anything.

options.text: Your belt. Look at both cats. Leave them where they are
options.result: You click in. You look at Gracie, then at Mya, and you know exactly where both of them are — which is loose on a seat, which is the truth. The belt is yours. It was only ever yours.

options.text: Put both cats in the carrier and call it done
options.result: You get Gracie in. By the time you've got Mya, Gracie's back on the seat. Ten minutes gone and your belt is still hanging by the pillar.

options.text: Belt Mya against the seat and leave Gracie
options.result: A cat is not a shape a seat belt understands. She's out of it before you've finished, and now the cab's worse and you're still unbuckled.

debrief: The belt is yours. Fasten it every time, before anything else moves.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Her belt, before the car moves. The cats ride loose. Wrong answers arm II-031.

variation.forced: live still cards/takes/I-003-take-1.png (cats on seat, belt from B-pillar, no 112; replaces lap+112 take-9)

title: Roll and Stop
hook: An empty aisle and nobody to be fast for.
scene: Painted stalls both sides, wet asphalt, the whole aisle to yourself. Nobody to beat, nobody waiting. Pick a line and see if you can stop on it.
decision: How do you move through the aisle?

options.text: Throttle, then brake at the end
options.result: You get there quickly and stop late and heavy, and both cats slide into the seat back. You arrived. You didn't stop where you meant to.

options.text: Roll, ease off early, stop on the line you picked
options.result: You let it roll, come off the throttle before you need to, and the car settles onto your line without asking anything of the brakes. Neither cat moves.

options.text: Creep the whole aisle with the brake half on
options.result: You ride it the full length. The car never settles into a roll, and you finish having fought the aisle instead of driven it.

options.text: Watch the cats and let the car find the end
options.result: You're looking at the seat when the stalls run out, so the stop isn't chosen — it's just where the paint got close.

debrief: Ease off before the stop. Smooth braking is a skill you build in a lot, before there's a street attached.

source.psdp_skill: Skill two: moving, steering, and stopping
source.teaching_target: Start, roll, and stop on a line she picked. Smooth.

title: Licensing Office, Kent
hook: Both cats on the seat. The doors are open.
scene: You parked in the Kent licensing lot because the license is the thing you came for. Gracie is on the passenger seat, cream chest, paws tucked. Mya is beside her, heavier, green eyes half shut. They came because they always come. The building is ahead through the mesh. The doors are propped. There is no line. There are no cars. The counter beyond the glass has nobody at it. The counter is empty. That is the end of the plan you drove here with. You have not gotten out yet.
debrief: You came for the license. The cats are with you because they always are. The doors are open and nobody is at the counter. That is as far as this goes.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Establish the DOL lot: she is here for the license, both cats are with her, and the building is wrong. End before she understands.

title: Gracie's Out
hook: Gracie is in the open lot. So are you.
scene: Gracie is out of the car and into the stalls, low and curious, ten feet off the open door. You are out after her. The Menace sits behind you, door hanging wide. Mya is still in the cab. Across the asphalt, about a hundred and twenty feet off, three figures are spread and moving at different angles. They are not coming toward you. None of them is looking at you.
decision: Gracie is in the open lot. How do you get her back?

options.text: Call her. Loudly. She knows your voice.
options.result: You call her name across the stalls. She stops. She turns. She knows you. The sound goes out over wet asphalt farther than the word did. She is coming back. You do not look at anything except her.

options.text: Get low, stay quiet, and move to cut her off from the open lot
options.result: You drop and stay low and do not use your voice. She is still moving, but she is not being called. You cut the open side of the lot and she slows when the space in front of her closes. You have her attention without the sound. That is the right way. It is not the only thing in the lot.

options.text: Go back for the carrier and come out with food
options.result: You go back to the car. The carrier is under the bench. By the time you have it and a bit of food, she is farther into the stalls than she was. The lot is still open. You spent the time you did not have.

options.text: Leave the car door open and wait — she'll come back on her own
options.result: You stay by the open door and wait. She does not come. The lot is not a place that waits with you. She gets farther into the painted stalls, and you are still standing where you started.

debrief: The call works. She turns. That is why you did it. The quiet cut-off is the one that does not send sound across the lot. Neither of those facts ends this.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Lot Quiet call-out — how you get the cat back. dol n/a: narrative/non-curriculum beat; not 5.5 Focus distraction.

title: The One You Didn't See
hook: You were watching the wrong three.
scene: You have Gracie. She's pulled tight against you, tense and low, ears back, head turned into your arm, orange and cream. Across the lot the three are still far off and still not looking. This one was never with them. It's already between the parked rows, coming mid-stride, head down, and you don't finish the thought before it stops short of you — short of her — and nothing touches either of you.
decision: It is coming. What do you do?

options.text: Put yourself between it and the cats
options.result: You turn so it has you and not her. Gracie is under your arm. It stops short. Nothing touches you. Nothing touches her. Mya is not here. You moved. It does not change what the lot takes.

options.text: Grab Gracie and run
options.result: You take Gracie and you go. She's against you. It's still coming when the moment breaks. Nothing touches you. Nothing touches her. You moved. The one that mattered was already closer than the three you were watching.

options.text: Freeze
options.result: You freeze. That is what a person does. Gracie is under your hand. It fills the near ground and then it is gone before it arrives. Nothing touches you. Nothing touches her. You did not choose this. You still get to have been here.

debrief: You had Gracie. The one that came was not one of the three. It never reached either of you.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Lunge beat once — lived experience, no grade. dol n/a: antagonist/narrative; no DOL curriculum home.

title: One of Them Comes Back
hook: One cat, where there were two.
scene: You are in the driver's seat. The door is shut. The engine is not started. Gracie is on your chest, shaking, orange and cream, both eyes open. The passenger seat is empty. You put the window down a little and say Mya's name, quietly, and then you stop, because calling is what started this. The lot behind the mesh is empty again. That is worse. You have Gracie. You are not hurt.
debrief: Sound draws them. You were loud because you were watching the wrong thing. Gracie is on your chest. The passenger seat is empty.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Sound draws them; end on empty seat. dol n/a: story rule / lot closer; not 5.5 Focus attention.

title: Before the Wheels
hook: You looked at this aisle twenty minutes ago.
scene: The engine's on. Gracie's on the seat in your lap now, still not settled. The passenger seat beside you is empty and you keep not looking at it. The aisle behind you is the way out, and the last time you saw it was before.
decision: Before you roll, what do you do?

options.text: Pull out. It was empty a minute ago.
options.result: You back out on a look you already spent. It might still be empty. You wouldn't know.

options.text: Look it again — both ways, and behind the bumper
options.result: Left, right, the row you're backing into, the ground behind you. Then you move, and the lot is clear because you checked, not because it was clear before.

options.text: Call her name once more, then go
options.result: Your voice goes out across the wet asphalt and nothing comes back, and you've spent the check on a name.

options.text: Sit with the empty seat until you're ready
options.result: You look at the seat for a while. The aisle goes unlooked-at the whole time.

debrief: Look before you move, every time. A clear lot goes stale in a minute.

source.psdp_skill: Skill one: before you start the engine
source.teaching_target: Look the aisle before she rolls. KEEP Skill one / n/a: pre-roll look; engine-on is scene continuity, not Skill two.

variation.forced: live still cards/takes/I-009-take-19.png (main↔prod reconcile; tip already live)

title: Out of the Stall
hook: Nose in. The way out is behind you.
scene: You parked pointed at a building you're not going into, which means leaving is a backing job — slow, one motion, into an aisle you can't see any of from where you're sitting.
decision: How do you get out of the stall?

options.text: Back out on the side mirror
options.result: The mirror gives you a slice of it. The corner of your own bumper isn't in that slice, and neither is the post you find.

options.text: Turn and look over your shoulder — slow, one motion
options.result: You twist in the seat, past the empty place beside you, and look at the actual aisle. The car comes out where you were looking.

options.text: Pull forward and cut across the stall line
options.result: You try to leave the way you're already pointed, end up across two stalls at an angle, and you're still not in the aisle.

options.text: Back out fast so it's over
options.result: You make it short by making it quick, and the aisle arrives before your look does.

debrief: Back up slowly, in one motion, looking over your shoulder at the aisle itself.

source.psdp_skill: Skill four: backing up
source.teaching_target: Back out of the stall by looking over the shoulder, slow, one motion. The mirror is not the look.

variation.forced: live still cards/takes/I-010-take-9.png (main↔prod reconcile; tip already live)

title: The Window
hook: She asks about the cats.
scene: Mom comes through on the radio, which she doesn't always. She asks if the cats are all right. You say Gracie is, and then you don't say the rest of it, and she doesn't ask. She tells you the pass is still closed like you might not have heard. You say you know. She doesn't ask how the driving is going. You don't tell her.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Mom is a voice. She asks about the cats and the pass. She does not ask how the driving is going. Ali says Gracie is and does not say the rest.

title: The Street
hook: You leave with one cat.
scene: You roll out onto a residential street with a twenty-five on it, which is the opposite of a mountain pass in every way that matters and the only place anybody has ever learned to drive one. The license isn't in your pocket. Gracie's on the seat. Somewhere out there is a cat with your name on her collar and no idea where you went, and the way you get back to either of them is the same way: this street, then the next one.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Close Act I. One sentence tying Mya, mom, and the curriculum. Quiet streets first.

title: Kent, Before First Light
hook: Insulin crates on the floor. The Grid still has paint.
scene: You idle at the curb on a Kent side street that still has its paint. The Menace ticks as it cools. Cranberry braid over one shoulder, wire rims catching the overcast, Gracie already on the dash with her paws in the defrost. Insulin crates sweat on the floor behind the seats. The Grid is residential, two lanes, stop signs that still mean stop. Signals still cycle. That is the whole job today: move the cold through streets that look empty and are not.
debrief: Act II is quiet Kent, not the lot. Search, signs, turns, bikes, buses, space, and focus — in that order. The lights still work. You took the cold through streets that still have rules.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Establish The Grid: residential Kent, Ali driving, insulin run, rules of the road still in force.

title: White Lights, Empty Yard
hook: School-zone lamps flash over a yard empty for months.
scene: The school-zone lamps are still lit on a Kent side street at dawn, white and cold, flashing over a dry playground that has not held a recess in fourteen months. Your speedo sits on twenty-eight. The painted 20 is faded but it is there. Nothing moves on the sidewalk. The insulin is still cold. The Menace wants the next block. Your eyes want the empty yard instead of the parked cars and the hedge line where a yard used to dump kids into the crosswalk.
decision: The lamps are flashing and the yard looks dead. Where do you put the speed?

options.text: Hold twenty-eight — nothing has used this crosswalk in a year
options.result: A courier on a dark bike comes out of the hedge line at the faded crosswalk without a lamp. You hit the brakes late on cold dry asphalt. The plow dips, the tires chirp, and the bike swerves around your left headlight. The sound carries. Two blocks down, something in a doorway turns its head.

options.text: Kill the lamps with a high-beam flash so you can see the yard
options.result: The flash punches white into the dawn. The school-zone lamps keep cycling. Every window on the block answers you. You did not slow. A shape that was sitting at the chain-link stands up and starts walking toward the light.

options.text: Drop to twenty and search the parked cars and hedge before the crosswalk
options.result: Twenty. Eyes left hedge, right parked bumpers, center faded lines. A kid's bike is on its side in the gutter, still, no rider. You roll the crosswalk at a walking pace and the zone lamps fall behind you. The Menace does not like twenty. The street does.

options.text: Cut through the empty lot to skip the zone entirely
options.result: The lot is frost-slick and rutted. The tires hop a concrete stop and the plow rings off it like a bell. You saved a block and spent it in noise. The school-zone lamps keep flashing for whoever is actually using the street.

debrief: When school-zone lights are flashing, the posted school speed is in force whether or not you can see children. Search the edges first — parked cars and hedges hide the thing that steps out. Ali holds twenty before the empty middle.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part one
source.teaching_target: Flashing school-zone lamps put the posted school speed in force; search parked cars and edges, not the empty center.

title: Red Octagon, White Fog
hook: Fog on torn-up road. A portable STOP sits in your lane.
scene: Fog sits on a Kent work zone at midday, thick enough that the cones appear one at a time. A portable stop sign is planted in your lane where the flagger would have stood. The face is red, eight sides, white border, white STOP. No flagger. No oncoming headlights yet. The cone line pinches you down to a crawl. The insulin clock is still kind. Your left foot wants to hover instead of plant.
decision: The portable stop is in your lane and the fog has the other approach. What do you do at the sign?

options.text: Full stop, count three, search both ways, then roll when the fog-lane is clear
options.result: You plant it. The Menace settles. Count one, two, three. A gray primer pickup slides out of the fog from the right at walking speed, never seeing you until you are already stopped. You let it pass, then take the gap. The sign did the flagger's job.

options.text: Rolling stop — tap the pedal and keep the crawl so you do not get stuck in the cones
options.result: You never quite reach zero. The primer pickup is already in the pinch. Your plow and his bumper occupy the same two feet of fog. A horn you did not mean to hit. Both of you freeze. The cones shake. Something at the far end of the zone turns toward the sound.

options.text: Treat it as yield and go if you cannot see anyone
options.result: You take the empty-looking gap. The pickup's left headlight fills your mesh at ten feet. Both of you dump speed. His tires bark on damp torn-up road. You sit in the intersection with two engines and a sign that already told you the answer.

options.text: Stop past the sign so you can see around the fog before committing
options.result: You roll the nose past the octagon to get a look. Now you are in the conflict box with no legal stop left to make. The pickup has to swerve around your plow. A cone goes over. Plastic on steel, sharp, and the fog carries it.

debrief: A stop sign means stop — wheels still, at the sign or limit line, even when the sign is portable and the road looks empty. Fog does not turn that into a yield. Stop at the sign, then search.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part one
source.teaching_target: Stop means a complete stop at the sign or limit line; a portable work-zone stop has the same force as a post.

title: Wind on Central
hook: Left pocket, blinker on. Oncoming is closing in the wind.
scene: The work cones are behind you. Central Avenue in Kent, two lanes each way, a protected left pocket painted and still honest. Wind shoves the Menace a half-lane toward the curb every time a gap opens. Oncoming is a primer SUV at distance and a lifted truck closer, closing. Your blinker has been on. The pocket is short. The insulin does not care about your gap. The oncoming does.
decision: You are in the left pocket with the blinker on. When do you take the turn?

options.text: Cut the wheels now and creep into the intersection so you can go the instant it opens
options.result: Wheels already left. The lifted truck never planned to stop. His bumper kisses your rear quarter and walks the Menace one foot into the oncoming lane. The SUV's horn is late. You are pointed at a collision you pre-steered yourself into.

options.text: Go now — the SUV is still far and the truck will brake for you
options.result: You take it. The truck does not brake. You are broadside in his closing speed with a plow that will not win. You dump the turn and abort back into the pocket, tires howling, wind shoving the tail. The SUV has to lift. Everyone on this block heard you decide.

options.text: Cancel the blinker and go right around the block instead
options.result: You kill the signal mid-pocket. The truck reads that as you staying put, then you yank right across his nose toward the through lane. He hits the horn. You make the block. You also taught the next driver that your blinker is optional.

options.text: Wheels straight, wait for the SUV and the truck both to clear, then turn
options.result: You hold the pocket. Wheels straight. The truck blows through. The SUV follows. The next gap is real. You turn on the blinker that was already telling the truth. Wind shoves the tail; you let it and unwind. No horn. No yaw. The crates do not slide.

debrief: For a left turn, wait until the whole gap is yours. Wheels stay straight until you commit so a rear-end does not push you into oncoming. Wheels straight in the pocket, blinker still on, both oncoming vehicles already past.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: Complete left turns only when oncoming is clear; keep wheels straight in the pocket until the turn is committed.

title: Marisol in the Lot
hook: A bike is closing on your left toward the same exit.
scene: Rain hammers the old Kent Station lot, a sheet off the mesh, the stalls faded to ghosts. You are rolling a lane of painted arrows toward the exit onto 1st. In the left side mirror, a bicycle: bare head, dark jacket, fast, unafraid. Marisol. She is using the lot as a cut-through the way she always has. She is on your left rear quarter — the driver's side — closing to pass you on the inside toward the same exit. Your window is up. Your door is a weapon if you forget she is there.
decision: Marisol is in your left mirror, coming up the driver's side toward the same exit. What do you do?

options.text: Hold your line and let her find a way around — the lot is yours
options.result: You occupy the arrow. She has to squeeze between your door and a cart corral. Her bar-end kisses the steel plating with a sound like a dropped wrench. She stays up. She also puts a hand out, not a wave. You taught a courier that cars do not look.

options.text: Slow, stay right of the arrows, and give her the whole left side through the exit
options.result: You lift and drift right inside the stall paint. She takes the left at speed, three clear feet of wet asphalt, and is through the exit before you. Two fingers off the bars without looking back. The rain covers the rest. You roll out after her at a walking pace.

options.text: Tap the horn so she knows you see her
options.result: The horn cracks off the storefront and the parking deck. Marisol flinches and the front wheel tucks. She saves it. Every Quiet thing using this lot as a sit has your range now. She looks at you once, jaw set, and takes the exit anyway.

options.text: Speed up to beat her to the exit and clear the conflict
options.result: You get there first by a car length. She is still on your left rear when you start the turn onto 1st. Your rear quarter walks through the space her front wheel needs. She bails onto the sidewalk and the bike hits a cart corral. Steel, loud, done.

debrief: Give bicyclists at least three feet when you share a space, more in rain. Check the left mirror, then give her the whole left side. A horn cost you the quiet lot.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Pass with ≥3 ft (4.6 exact). Skill six is a soft look-ahead wrapper for finding her in the mirror.

title: Deac's Left Arm
hook: Deac's arm goes straight, then down. Someone is on your bumper.
scene: Night has dropped on a Kent school zone that still flashes for no one. You are second in a two-vehicle run: the Ledger ahead, amber destination sign dark, the big west-coast mirrors on his doors. Deac's left arm comes out the driver's window, straight out, then down — the old transit slow. Radios are trash. That is how he talks. A third set of lamps sits on your bumper, too close, some volunteer who joined without asking. Gracie is boxed. Your job is not to be clever. Your job is to answer him without lighting the block.
decision: Deac's left arm is out and down. The volunteer behind you is tight. How do you answer?

options.text: Match him: left arm out and down, lift off, and open a gap ahead of the volunteer
options.result: You answer in kind. The Menace slows without the brake lamps dumping. The volunteer has to lift or eat your plow. He lifts. Deac's arm comes back in. The three of you roll the zone at twenty, dark and boring. That is a successful convoy.

options.text: Flash your headlights twice so Deac knows you saw it
options.result: The flashes bounce off his expanded-metal rear and paint the playground. Deac's arm stays down because he was not asking for a receipt. At the treeline, two shapes that were sitting stand up and start to walk the fence toward the light.

options.text: Tap the brakes hard so the volunteer gets the message
options.result: Your lamps dump red into his windshield. He stands on his own brakes. Three vehicles, one wet school zone, a squeal. Deac's arm comes back in and the destination sign flickers one word you cannot read from here. You just talked over him.

options.text: Pass him on the left and take the point — he is going too slow for the insulin
options.result: You pull out in a flashing school zone. His left arm is still in the air you are occupying. The Ledger's mirror almost takes your mesh. He never speeds up. You are now point on a road you have not searched, with a volunteer still glued to Deac, and no one behind you speaking the same language.

debrief: Left arm out, fingers pointing at the ground, means slow or stop. Answer with the same arm and a smooth lift. Deac asked for slow, not a receipt.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: Left arm out and down means slow or stop; answer a convoy signal with the same hand signal and a smooth deceleration.

title: Bus 12, Amber
hook: Bus 12's ambers just came on. The left lane is open.
scene: Fourth Ave South, Kent, and the rain has been going since Renton. Half a block up, Bus 12 rolls at maybe fifteen. Reyna runs the last shelter route and she runs it on time. The amber lamps come on above her rear window. Gracie stands up in the passenger footwell. You are carrying insulin that has a hundred and ten minutes of cold left, and there is a clear lane to Reyna's left.
decision: The amber lamps are on and the left lane is open. What do you do?

options.text: Take the left lane and get past her before the reds come on
options.result: You are alongside the front bumper when the reds fire and the stop arm swings into your door line. The plow catches it. Steel on steel, and the sound goes out across four blocks of flat wet street. Reyna does not blow the horn. She does not have to.

options.text: Ease off and start slowing now, staying behind her
options.result: You lift and let the gap open to four car lengths. The reds come on, the arm swings out, and a kid in a yellow shell comes around the front of the bus at a dead sprint without looking once. He is across before you have finished counting him. Reyna gives you two fingers off the wheel.

options.text: Hold your speed and stay behind — you'll stop when the reds come on
options.result: You are still at twenty-eight when the reds fire. Hard on the brakes, wet asphalt, and the Menace squats and squeals to a stop with the plow eight feet off her bumper. You stopped legally. You also just rang a bell on a quiet street, and something moves at the treeline four blocks down.

options.text: Flash your headlights so Reyna knows you're behind her
options.result: The flash bounces off the wet street and every window on the block. Reyna's hand comes out the window, flat, palm down — cut it. The reds fire anyway, and you brake late because you were watching her hand instead of her lamps.

debrief: Amber lamps mean the bus is preparing to stop. That is your cue to slow, not a last chance to pass. Red lamps plus the stop arm mean a full stop from both directions until the arm comes back in. Wait behind her until the arm folds.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Amber lamps signal an approaching stop; red lamps and extended stop arm require a full stop from both directions.

title: Oil on Torn-Up Road
hook: Oil light's on. A dark fan sits in the mirror.
scene: The oil light is a dull orange you have been ignoring since the lot. Fog again, a Kent work zone that never got new pavement, cones still in a lazy line. You feel the note change — not a knock, a dry rattle under the rear. A dark fan of oil is already on the torn-up road behind you in the mirror, too even to be rain. The insulin is still in the window. The engine is not. Nobody is coming to tow the Menace. The Quiet will, if you sit in the travel lane and cook it.
decision: The oil light is on and you are laying a fan on the torn-up road. Where do you put the car?

options.text: Keep rolling to the next side street so you do not stop in the work zone
options.result: Two more blocks. The rattle becomes a bang. The Menace dies in the pinch between cones with no shoulder. You are a pink wreck in a fogged lane. Something at the torn-up edge already has your heat.

options.text: Rev it to climb the oil pressure back before you decide
options.result: The note screams and then stops. You have a seized engine and a still-rolling car. You coast into a cone and the plow rings. Fog holds the sound. The light was not a suggestion.

options.text: Signal, get off the torn-up road onto the gravel shoulder, shut it down, then check
options.result: Blinker. Gravel. Key off. The rattle dies with the engine. Under the rear, a split line, not a hole in the pan. You have tape and a bottle in the wing. Ten quiet minutes. The fog does not care. The engine will start once. That is enough to finish the run.

options.text: Stop in the lane, pop the deck, and look while it is still hot
options.result: You are standing in a fogged work lane with the deck up and a hot engine ticking. A volunteer comes through the cone line on your closed side and has to swerve. His horn. Your hood is a sail. You learn nothing you could not have learned on the shoulder, and now two vehicles are advertising.

debrief: An oil warning means get out of the travel lane, then shut down, then look. Keep rolling and you turn a split line into a dead vehicle sitting in the road. A pink roof in the fog, engine ticking, no oil pressure.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Heed oil and temperature warnings immediately; leave the travel lane, shut down, then inspect.

title: A Voice You Know
hook: The radio bleeds by itself. Someone is already in the crosswalk.
scene: The radio bleeds at dawn on a Kent two-lane. Wind again. You did not turn the radio on. It came up by itself, a trick the aftermarket tablet has been pulling since the lot — a scrap of a familiar voice, half a word, then static. The Chorus. Your eyes drop to the tablet the way they always do. A four-way is coming. A pedestrian in a hood is already in the crosswalk from the right, mid-block enough to be easy to miss if you are looking down. Both hands should be on the wheel. One of them is not.
decision: The tablet is talking in a voice you know and a pedestrian is in the crosswalk. Where do your eyes go?

options.text: Look down long enough to kill the tablet, then look back up
options.result: Two seconds on the tablet. The hood is already at your right headlight when you come back. You stand on the pedal. The Menace squats. The pedestrian does not run. They do not have to. You stopped a plow's width short, loud, and the tablet is still talking.

options.text: Answer the voice — if it is someone on the net they may have a better route
options.result: You unkey and talk into a tablet that is not a radio. The pedestrian is gone under the mesh before you finish the sentence. You missed them completely. The voice was never going to answer. That is the whole trick.

options.text: Speed up through the intersection so you are past the distraction sooner
options.result: You take the four-way hot. The pedestrian stops and the hood turns. You miss them by luck and a lot of wind. The tablet keeps talking. Speed did not buy attention. It spent the margin you needed.

options.text: Eyes up, both hands on the wheel, cover the brake, ignore the tablet until you are through
options.result: You leave the tablet alone. Hands at ten and two, or whatever your braid allows. The hood clears your right fender while you are still moving at a crawl. The tablet talks to itself and then dies. The hood is already on the far curb.

debrief: Eyes off the road — even to silence a distraction — is how the crash happens. Drive first. Park the tablet until the intersection is behind you. You missed the hood the second you looked down.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Do not take your eyes off the road to manage a device; drive through the hazard, then deal with the distraction.

title: The Arm Still Out
hook: Reds on, stop arm out. Tobin is already in the street.
scene: Bus 12 is back on Fourth Ave South at Willis, same rain, same crown in the wheel tracks, same bare maples. Reyna has the reds on and the stop arm is out — bent a few degrees off true from a plow that did not wait. Tobin is already in the street this time, yellow shell, not looking. At the treeline four blocks down, something that heard steel on steel last time has not left. This time you are the oncoming car: same reds, same arm, a lane that looks open and is not yours. The insulin can wait. He cannot.
decision: Reds are on, the arm is out, and Tobin is in the lane. What do you do?

options.text: Stay stopped until the arm folds, even though you are not behind her
options.result: You sit. Rain on the mesh. Tobin crosses without a glance, then a second kid you did not have last time. The thing at the treeline does not come. Reyna folds the bent arm, finds you in her mirror, and does not wave. She does not have to. You are still here. That is the apology.

options.text: Keep rolling — you are oncoming, so the reds are hers
options.result: You pull out on reds. Tobin is still in your left headlight. You stand on it. The Menace stops with the plow in the crosswalk he is using. Reyna sees the whole thing in her big school-bus mirror. She has a bent arm and a face you will carry.

options.text: Creep past the arm on the right shoulder to get out of the thing at the treeline's sightline
options.result: The gravel shoulder puts you around the bent arm and into the space kids use. A backpack scrapes the plating. You are past the bus and still in the rain, and the treeline has you in profile, moving. You did not get quieter. You got closer.

options.text: Tap the horn once so Tobin looks up
options.result: The horn on a stopped bus street. Tobin looks. So does everything else. The treeline starts walking. Reyna's head turns in the mirror, not grateful. You made him look and you rang the block doing it.

debrief: Red lamps and an extended stop arm still mean a full stop from both directions until the arm comes back in — even when you have been here before, even when the arm is bent because of you. Reyna is still watching that bent arm.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Red lamps and an extended stop arm require a full stop from both directions until the arm retracts; never pass a stopped school bus.

variation.forced: location+weather+time locked to II-007 callback; camera POV_ROADSIDE so the bus ahead is not compiled into a rearview

title: Write the Hours Down
hook: Deac's clipboard is on the floor. Write the hours down.
scene: You unfold a metal clipboard that is not yours. Deac left it on the floor at the lot with a note in dispatch cadence: date, location, day or night, weather, skills, hours, initials. The Grid does not count as practice unless you write it down. Clear cold midday in a Kent lot, stalls faded, the Menace ticking. You have already used a school zone, a stop, a left, a bike, a bus, a hand, a light, a voice. The clipboard is how the hours become legal. It is also how you notice you have not done space yet.
debrief: Supervised hours live on the log: date, location, day or night, weather, skill, time, initials. Keep the hours on the sheet.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Hours only count when written down. Space cushion is the next unpaid skill.

title: Three Seconds, Not One
hook: You can see his hitch. You should be seeing pavement.
scene: A volunteer van is glued to a Kent school-zone exit at dusk, overcast, lamps already flashing for a shift that will not come. You are behind him. He is behind a dead sedan that is actually just parked badly. Your following gap is a bumper. The clipboard said space. The van's brake lamps are already dirty. If he dumps them, you will eat his trailer hitch with a plow that rings. The insulin is stable. Your right foot is not. You can see his tires. You should be able to see pavement.
decision: You can only see his hitch. How much road do you put back?

options.text: Stay on him so nobody cuts in — this zone is too narrow for a real gap
options.result: He dumps the brakes for a cat. You dump yours for him. The plow kisses the hitch. Not a crash. A note. The school-zone lamps keep flashing over a sound that did not need to happen.

options.text: Lift until you can count three seconds off a mark on the pavement, then hold that
options.result: You let him go. A faded crack in the asphalt passes his bumper; you count one-one-thousand, two, three, then take the throttle back. You can see his tires and the road under them. When he does dump it, you are already covering. No note. No kiss.

options.text: Pass him in the zone so you are not the one eating the hitch
options.result: You pull out flashing. He drifts right from surprise. You make the pass and inherit the parked sedan as your new hitch. The lamps saw the whole thing. So did whatever uses this fence after dusk.

options.text: Close up and flash him once to tell him to move
options.result: The flash fills his glass. He brakes from the insult. You are closer than when you started. He never had a place to go. You just asked a following-distance problem to become a light problem.

debrief: Following distance is counted in seconds. Dry pavement: three to a mark on the road. Rain, fog, and snow: six. Rear-end crashes are the most common kind. Opening that gap is the best thing a new driver can do. A mark on the pavement, then one, two, three.

source.psdp_skill: Skill three: how close are you?
source.teaching_target: Three seconds is the dry-road following baseline; if you cannot see pavement under the vehicle ahead, you are too close.
source.stat_cited: PSDP p.11: Rear-end collisions are the most common form of a car crash; increasing following distance is the single best thing a new driver can do to reduce crash risk.

title: Orange Triangle Ahead
hook: Orange triangle ahead in the cones. You are doing thirty.
scene: Heavy rain at night on a Kent work zone, cones still in the lane. In the cone line, a farm tractor from somebody's last run south, no Grange, just one machine, orange slow-vehicle triangle dirty but lit by your lamps. It is doing twelve. You are doing thirty because the insulin clock got loud in your head. The triangle is the sign. Pass on a two-lane with no sightline and you are in his blind spot and oncoming's. The cones make it worse. Your left blinker already wants out.
decision: The slow-moving triangle is ahead in the cones. Do you pass?

options.text: Pass now — twelve is not a speed and the insulin is not a suggestion
options.result: You pull out in the rain. The tractor occupies more width than it looks. Oncoming is a pair of lamps you did not have. You dive back in and clip a cone. The triangle fills your glass. You saved nothing and spent a lot of noise.

options.text: Flash him to pull into the cones so you can go
options.result: The flash hits the triangle and comes back at you twice as bright. He has nowhere to pull. He brakes. You almost eat the hitch of a machine that cannot get out of your way because you asked it to.

options.text: Stay behind, drop to his twelve, and wait for a marked passing zone with sight
options.result: You lift to twelve. The cone line ends. A painted passing zone appears with a sightline you can actually see. You take it then, clean, and leave him a gap. The insulin is still cold. Twelve cost you a minute. A pass in the rain would have cost the run.

options.text: Go around on the gravel because the lane is his
options.result: The gravel is a ditch in the rain. The tires climb and the plow drops. You are beside him in a trench with no legal lane. He never saw you. The first thing he knows is your roof in his left mirror and a sound like a drum.

debrief: An orange triangle marks a machine doing farm speed. Pass only where the paint allows it and you can see. Twelve cost you a minute.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: The orange triangle marks a slow vehicle; pass only where passing is legal and sight distance is enough.

title: Hollis in the Glass
hook: Hollis sits a bumper off your rear in the fog.
scene: Fog on a Kent four-lane in the morning. In the inside mirror, a lifted truck with aftermarket lamps sits a bumper off your rear. Hollis. He has been there for six blocks. He wants you faster than the fog. Your speedo is already at the number on the sign. If you dump speed he will eat you. If you give him the number he wants, the fog will. The left lane is a rumor in this weather. Gracie is boxed. Your mirrors are the whole conversation.
decision: Hollis is a bumper off you in the fog. How do you keep the space?

options.text: Ease a little off the throttle to rebuild the gap ahead, and refuse to match him
options.result: You bleed three miles per hour, nothing dramatic. The gap ahead opens. Hollis fills it, then thinks about your bumper, then finally goes around when a gap appears. His pass is ugly and close. You let it be ugly. You still have a following distance to the gray nothing in front of you.

options.text: Match his pressure and take the fog at his speed so he will back off
options.result: You give him the number. The fog does not. A parked car appears at twenty feet. You stand on it. Hollis stands on you. Three vehicles, one note, a chain that started because you let a tailgater set the limit.

options.text: Brake-check him once so he learns the gap
options.result: You dump the lamps in his face. He dumps his. The Menace hops. His bumper kisses the plating. Fog holds the sound. He did not learn. He got closer, angrier, and louder.

options.text: Wave him around and drift right onto the fogged shoulder to make a lane
options.result: There is no shoulder, only a ditch. The tires find it. You yaw. Hollis takes the space you were occupying and never looks back. You spend a minute getting the plow back onto asphalt that you already had.

debrief: You do not speed up for a tailgater. Fog wants six seconds ahead, not the dry three. Bleed a little speed to rebuild that gap. Hollis can take the pass when a gap opens.

source.psdp_skill: Skill three: how close are you?
source.teaching_target: Do not increase speed for a tailgater; in fog hold six seconds ahead and allow a pass when it is legal.

title: Right, After the Hedge
hook: You need the right. A hedge hides the sidewalk.
scene: Wind at dawn on a Kent residential that dead-ends into a T. You need the right. A hedge on the corner hides the sidewalk. Your blinker has been on for a block because Deac's voice in your head still counts cadence. A cyclist you cannot yet see will be on that sidewalk if this is that kind of morning. You need to see past the hedge before you commit the nose. The Menace's plow makes every early turn longer than it looks.
decision: The hedge hides the right sidewalk. When do you start the turn?

options.text: Start the turn at the hedge so you can peek the sidewalk with the plow
options.result: The plow is in the crosswalk before you can see it. Marisol is not here this time. A kid on a scooter is. You freeze with steel in his path. He stops. You have taught the corner that cars occupy the sidewalk to see.

options.text: Cut the corner tight to stay out of whoever is on the far side
options.result: You take the turn in their sidewalk. The tires climb the curb. The plow rings off a fire hydrant nobody has painted in a year. Tight was not smaller. Tight was on the wrong side of the geometry.

options.text: Skip the turn and go left around the block where you can see
options.result: You kill a blinker that had been telling the truth and take an unsignaled left at a T. The through car you did not have honks. You make the block. You also skipped the skill the corner was for.

options.text: Stop at the sidewalk line, search around the hedge, then turn into the nearest right lane
options.result: You stop short of the sidewalk. The hedge still hides a slice. You creep until the slice is a view. Empty. You take the nearest right lane, wide enough that the plow does not climb the curb. The blinker dies when the wheel unwinds. Boring. Correct.

debrief: Right turns yield to the sidewalk and crosswalk first. If a hedge hides the sightline, search before the nose occupies it. Stop at the sidewalk line, then take the nearest right lane.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: Before a right turn, search the sidewalk and crosswalk; do not start the turn until the path is visible; recover into the nearest right lane.

title: The Arm Points Left
hook: Deac's arm is straight left. The volunteer is third.
scene: Rain at midday in the Kent Station lot again, different stalls, same wet deck. Deac has the Ledger pointed at the exit, amber sign dark. He needs a left onto 1st. His left arm comes out the driver window and holds, straight, fingers pointing left into the rain — not bent, not up. You are second. A volunteer is third. If you signal with lamps you light the deck. If you say nothing, the volunteer will read the gap on Deac's left as an opening and take the turn with him. Hands are the only signal that does not light the lot.
decision: Deac's left arm is straight out. How do you keep the volunteer off his left?

options.text: Flash twice and pull left so the volunteer stays put
options.result: The flashes paint the deck. The volunteer reads it as go and comes around you into Deac's left. Three vehicles in an exit that holds two. Deac's arm is still out in a space that is no longer his.

options.text: Left arm straight out to match, hold your place, and do not open a gap on his left
options.result: You put the same arm out the same window. You stay glued to his right-rear, not his left. The volunteer has no gap that is not a curb. Deac takes the left. You take it after him. The volunteer waits because the line was complete.

options.text: Bend the arm up — that is the left-turn he meant
options.result: Your arm goes up. His stays flat. The volunteer copies you, not him, and starts a right that nobody called. Deac has to drop the turn. You taught the wrong sky to a man who was pointing at the street.

options.text: Horn once, short, so the volunteer freezes
options.result: The horn in a parking deck. Everyone freezes, including Deac. The Quiet using the far stairwell does not. You bought a second and spent the block.

debrief: A left turn is the left arm straight out the driver-side window, fingers pointing left. Match Deac on that side and stay off his left. You took the left after him, not beside him.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: Left turn: left arm out the driver window, straight, fingers pointing left; match convoy signals and do not leave a gap on the turning side.

title: Solid Yellow, Do Not Pass
hook: A van crawls ahead, dead slow. The yellow on your side is solid.
scene: Clear cold afternoon. A Kent school zone with a solid yellow on your side. A delivery van crawls ahead of you, dead slow through the zone. Passing would put you over the solid. The playground is empty. The line is not. Hollis is not in this one. Nobody is coming the other way that you can see. That is the trick of a solid yellow: the thing you cannot see yet still owns that paint.
decision: A dead-slow van is blocking your speed and the yellow under you is solid. Do you go around?

options.text: Stay behind the van until you can pass where the yellow breaks, even if that is slow
options.result: You wait. A block later the yellow breaks. You check, pass, and recover before the next solid. A car you did not have comes the other way in the gap you would have occupied. The van stays dead slow. You stay in your lane.

options.text: Go around now — nothing is coming and the van is the real hazard
options.result: You cross the solid. The other car was in the school-zone dip. Two plows of width, one lane, a freeze. You dive back and scrape the van. Paint on primer. The yellow was not decorative.

options.text: Straddle the yellow to peek, then decide
options.result: You are already in their lane to peek. Peeking is occupying. The dip car has to take the curb. You learned the sightline by stealing it.

options.text: Use the parking lane on the right to sneak past without crossing yellow
options.result: The parking lane is a door zone of ghosts. A van door that was not quite latched opens into your mesh. You pass the delivery van and inherit a different one. Right was not free. It was unsearched.

debrief: A solid yellow on your side means do not pass. Wait for the broken yellow and a sightline. The dead-slow van is a delay. Ali waits until the yellow breaks.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part one
source.teaching_target: Do not pass on a solid yellow line on your side; wait for a broken line and adequate sight distance.

title: Box Her Before You Roll
hook: Gracie is on the dash. Box her before you roll.
scene: You unclip the carrier in a Kent work zone at dusk, overcast, cones leaning like they are tired. Gracie hits the dash like she owns the defrost. Orange tabby, cream chest, amber-green eyes, already in the way of the right side mirror. This is the passenger problem with a face. She will stand up at the wrong bus. She will walk a keyboard you do not have. The Grid still has eight cards of space and night and ice in it. If she is loose, she is a lap. If she is boxed, she is a sound you can ignore. You have to choose before the next roll, not during it.
decision: Gracie is on the dash. What do you do before you roll?

options.text: Clip her back in the carrier and stow it before you roll
options.result: You box her. The clip bites. She complains once and then she is a sound on the floor next to the seat, not a face on the glass. Your eyes stay on the torn-up road, not on a cream chest that wants the defrost.

options.text: Leave her. She will settle once the Menace starts rolling
options.result: She does not settle. She stands into the right side mirror as you enter the work zone. Your eyes go to her. The cone line does not wait. A cone kisses the plow with a note you will hear next to the seat for a block.

options.text: Pull her into your lap so she is off the glass
options.result: Mass in your legs. She kneads. Your right foot is a negotiation. A work zone does not care that you have a cat. You wander an inch and the cone line teaches you the width of a lap.

options.text: Let her walk the dash. You can watch her and the cones at once
options.result: You cannot. She takes the defrost. Your eyes leave the cones. The next cone is closer than the last one looked. Two jobs, one pair of eyes, and the work zone does not pause for cream fur.

debrief: Unrestrained passengers — including a cat — are a distraction with mass. Eyes that go to the dash leave the cones. Clip her in, then roll.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Restrain pets before roll (4.19 Animals). Loose animals distract; not a 5.5 Focus catch-all.

title: Green Light, Black Ice
hook: The paint looks wet. It is ice. The light is green.
scene: Night on a Kent two-lane that iced after a melt. The paint still looks wet. It is not. Your tires are honest until they are not. A four-way with a working signal, stale green. You are the only moving thing. The instinct is to take the green like you own it. The ice wants a smaller number and no sudden anything. The insulin crates will slide if you ask the tires for more than they can give. There is no sand truck. There is you, a green lamp, and a surface that will not say its name until you brake.
decision: The lamp is green and the paint looks only wet. How do you take the intersection?

options.text: Take it at town speed — green means you have the intersection
options.result: You ask the tires for twenty-eight. They give you yaw. The Menace rotates a quarter turn in the crosswalk and slides under the green like a joke. You miss the pole. The crates do not miss the sidewall. The Quiet will hear the rest.

options.text: Stab the brakes before the painted line to test the ice
options.result: The test is the crash. Locked tires, a plow that now points at a dark porch, and a green lamp still cycling for a car that is no longer in its lane. You learned the ice by using up the intersection.

options.text: Bleed speed early, no brake in the ice, and roll the green at a walking pace
options.result: You lift a block out. No stab. The Menace settles into a crawl that looks foolish and is not. The green is still green when you take it straight, hands quiet. The crates stay put. The lamp did not make the ice optional.

options.text: Stop fully and wait for the next green so you can start from zero on ice
options.result: You stop on ice under a green. Starting from zero on ice is a different failure. The tires spin, the plow walks left, and the next cycle finds you still in the box. You turned a through into a stall.

debrief: Green tells you who has the intersection. Ice wants six seconds of space and a walking pace — bleed before the box, no sudden anything. The green lamp is still there when you roll through.

source.psdp_skill: Skill three: how close are you?
source.teaching_target: On ice, take six seconds of space and bleed speed before the box; do not brake or turn suddenly, even on a green.

title: One Lamp in the Rain
hook: The left headlamp is dead. The right still works.
scene: Heavy rain on a Kent residential at morning, the kind that turns every surface into a mirror. Your left headlamp has been dying for a mile — a yellow wink, then dark. The right is still a proper low beam. High beams would fill the rain and give you nothing but scatter, and they would give the Quiet a lighthouse. You have a spare sealed beam in the wing that takes two hands and a shoulder. You also have a running lane. The legal requirement is two lamps at night or in rain. The tactical requirement is not to stand in the street to be correct.
decision: The left lamp is dead in the rain. What do you do before the next mile?

options.text: Pull onto a driveway, shut down, swap the sealed beam, then roll on lows
options.result: You do the legal thing in the travel-adjacent. The hood is up in the rain. A volunteer comes around the curve and has to take your door line. You get the lamp on. You also spent five loud minutes being a pink island.

options.text: Hit the highs so at least one side is bright enough to count as two
options.result: The rain blooms. You cannot see past the scatter. Every window on the block has you. The dead left is still dead. You made a lighting problem into a drawing problem.

options.text: Keep rolling — one lamp is enough if you stay under twenty
options.result: A courier in dark kit cannot see your left edge. They take it as a motorcycle. Your plow teaches them otherwise at a driveway. One lamp was not a vehicle. It was a rumor.

options.text: Get off the street into a driveway well off the travel lane, then swap the beam on lows only
options.result: You take a driveway that is actually a driveway, not a shoulder. Key off. Two minutes, rain on the plating, sealed beam seated. Lows, both sides. You back out after a search. The Quiet never got a lighthouse. The next car can count you as a car.

debrief: Two working headlights in rain. High beams bloom on the drops and give you scatter. You saved the swap for a driveway off the street.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Headlights must work in pairs in rain and dark; repair off the roadway; do not use high beams in heavy rain.

title: Back Out of the Fog
hook: Nosed in, fog in the stalls. You have to back out.
scene: Fog at dawn in a Kent lot, stalls so faded you are guessing with the wheel. You nosed in because the drop was at the shutter. Now you have to back out to leave. A row of dead cars on both sides. Your rear mesh is a cage, not a window. The side mirrors are honest if you use them. A bicycle wheel you cannot see from the seat will be in the backup path if this is Marisol's morning. It is not her, not yet. It is a cart corral that moved in the night. Backing is the skill people skip because going forward feels like progress.
decision: You are nosed in, in fog, and you have to leave. How do you back out?

options.text: Throw it in reverse and go — the lot was empty when you pulled in
options.result: The corral is not where it was. The plow is the wrong end for this. The rear plating hits steel and rings. You still cannot see what you hit until you get out. Fog holds the note.

options.text: Both side mirrors, look behind, creep reverse, stop if anything appears, then finish the out
options.result: Right glass, left glass, a look through the mesh that shows you almost nothing, then an inching reverse. The corral is there. You stop, wheel, and miss it by a foot. Fog. Boring. You are in the aisle pointed at the exit, which is the whole point of backing.

options.text: Cut a Y-turn in the stall so you can leave forward
options.result: There is not a Y-turn's worth of stall. You climb a parking bumper and the plow rings. Forward felt better. Geometry disagreed.

options.text: Get out and walk the path, then back out without checking again
options.result: You walk it. Clear. You get in and reverse on memory. In the ten seconds you were in the seat, a volunteer rolled a pallet into your path. Memory is not a mirror.

debrief: Backing is searching, then creeping. Mirrors and a look behind, every time, even in a lot you just used. Walking the path helps; it does not replace the last look. The aisle is empty and you are pointed at the exit.

source.psdp_skill: Skill eight: parking – part one
source.teaching_target: Before backing, search mirrors and behind the vehicle; back slowly and be ready to stop; do not rely on a walk-around done in the past tense.

title: Bent Arm, Right Turn
hook: Deac's left arm bends up. The volunteer rolls straight.
scene: Wind at midday through a Kent school zone, lamps dark this time, posted 20 still posted. You are third behind a volunteer and the Ledger. Deac's left arm comes out his driver window and bends at the elbow until the fingers point at the sky — rain hitting the sleeve, on the side the column can see. He cannot put this on the destination sign. The volunteer in the middle does not answer. His blinker never happens. If you follow the middle car you will miss the driveway on the right. If you put an arm out the passenger window, nobody behind you will see it.
decision: Deac's left arm is bent up in the rain. The volunteer is rolling straight. What do you do?

options.text: Match him: left arm out, bent up, and take the right after he does — do not follow the volunteer
options.result: Your left arm goes out into the same wind. The volunteer rolls straight. You do not. You take Deac's right after a gap. Two vehicles in a driveway that holds two. He put the signal on the side you could see. You answered on that side.

options.text: Stay glued to the volunteer — he is the one in front of you
options.result: You follow the man who missed the arm. Deac turns. You and the volunteer continue. Now the column is split and you are point on a road Deac did not want. The insulin is in the wrong driveway.

options.text: Put your right arm out the passenger window so the driveway side gets the signal
options.result: The arm is on the curb side. Deac cannot see it. The volunteer cannot see it. You look busy and you are mute. He turns without you. You taught the column a signal the guide does not have.

options.text: Pass both on the left and take the right first to hold the driveway
options.result: You occupy Deac's turn from the wrong side of a school zone. He has to wait on you. The volunteer follows you because movement is easier than an arm in the rain. You are point. You did not earn it.

debrief: Every hand signal is the left arm, out the driver window. Bent up, fingers to the sky, is a right turn. Copy the arm you can see. You took the right after the volunteer rolled straight.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: Right turn: left arm out the driver window, bent at the elbow, fingers pointing up; there is no right-arm hand signal.

title: Do Not Stop in the Cut
hook: A pickup sits dead in the only live lane.
scene: Afternoon rain on a slide cut — not Kent Station, a wet rock wall with one lane open and the other a trench behind cones. A pickup is already stopped in the open lane with its hood up, two people standing at the hood in the travel path. There is no shoulder that is not a drop. Your instinct is to wait behind them, which makes you the third body in a lane that still has a through. The sign at the start of the zone said DO NOT STOP. It meant it. You need an opening that is not their repair.
decision: They are stopped in the only live lane. Where do you put the Menace?

options.text: Wait behind them with hazards on so the next car sees a line
options.result: Hazards in a trench. The next car does see you. So does everything that hunts lamps. You are now a parked line in a work zone that forbade stopping. The pickup never asked you to join the repair.

options.text: Squeeze past them in the trench because you cannot stop
options.result: The tires drop off the cut. You high-center on the lip. Now there are two dead vehicles in a one-lane zone, and you are the second one.

options.text: Stop short of their scene, then wait in their lane until they move
options.result: You are polite and you are a blockage. A volunteer comes the other way in a lane that was supposed to be yours. Four people, one trench, no way through.

options.text: Do not stop in the zone: take the first legal turnout before the cut, then a different street
options.result: You refuse the line. A driveway before the cones is a driveway. You reverse into it, wait for an opening that is not their hood, and take the next street south. Two people stay at the pickup. You are already gone.

debrief: Do not stop in a live work lane to stare or to join someone else's breakdown. If the lane is blocked, leave the zone at the first legal turnout and go another way. Ali leaves the cut at the first driveway.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Never stop or park in a live work-zone travel lane; leave the zone and reroute if the lane is blocked.

title: First In at the Four-Way
hook: Four-way stop. The sedan on your right was there first.
scene: Clear cold dusk on a Kent four-way that still has all four stops. You arrive second. A primer sedan is already stopped on your right, a beat longer than you. Nobody else. The insulin is a minute from the shelter drop. The sedan's driver is not moving. They may be looking at a paper. They may be waiting for you to steal the opening. First in is first through. Your right is not a permission slip if they were there first. The Menace's idle is a drum if you rev it. You do not.
decision: You rolled up second. The sedan on your right is first and still sitting. Who goes through first?

options.text: Take it — they froze, and the drop will not wait
options.result: You go. They go. The two of you occupy the same paint. A freeze, a horn, a miss by a plow's width. First-in was not a suggestion. You made it a coin flip.

options.text: Wave them through even if you think you were first
options.result: You wave. They wave. Nobody goes. Then you both go. Courtesy without a rule is two people guessing. The intersection stays a mess for a third car that did not exist until it did.

options.text: Inch into the box to claim it so they have to wait
options.result: Your plow is in the conflict. They have to go around it or sit. They sit, then panic-go. You taught the four-way that steel is right-of-way. It is not.

options.text: Stay stopped. They were first. When they take it, you go next
options.result: You wait. They were looking at a paper. They look up, take the opening, and leave you a clean four-way. You take it. No horn. The drop is one minute later and still a drop.

debrief: At an all-way stop, the first vehicle to arrive goes first. If two arrive together, yield to the right. Waving is how two people enter the box at once. Wait out a frozen driver until they move.

source.psdp_skill: Skill five: driving on a quiet street – part two
source.teaching_target: All-way stop: first to arrive goes first; if simultaneous, yield to the right; do not occupy the box to force the issue.

title: Night on a Kent Curb
hook: Ordinary dark on a Kent curb. The rules still hold.
scene: You sit at a curb on a Kent residential that has gone overcast-night, not the Dark Hours yet, just the ordinary dark the Grid always had. Signals still cycle. A stale green somewhere to the west paints the wet. Ali in the glass: braid, wire rims, the pink hoodie gone gray in this light. The clipboard next to the seat has hours on it now. School zones. Stops. Turns. Bikes. A bus you may have passed. Space. Ice. A cut you refused to join. The Quiet uses the same paint at night. The rules do not get optional when the color drains. Tomorrow is more of this, then it is not — then it is someone else's act.
debrief: Night in The Grid is still The Grid. Lights work. Search harder. The Dark Hours are a later zone. The hoodie is gray and the lamps still cycle.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Night does not suspend residential rules; Act II remains search, space, and communication until the zone is clean.

title: Look Before the Door
hook: Ice in the lot. Marisol is in the aisle your door wants.
scene: Ice in the Kent Station lot at morning, the stalls a rink. You stopped along a row of dead cars to make the last drop on foot. Marisol is coming up the painted aisle in the left side mirror, from behind, slow because ice, still unafraid. Your door is the next thing she will occupy if you open it like a person who is late. Far hand on the handle turns your body to look, then you open. Your left hand wants the handle because you have always opened a door with that hand. The insulin crate is in your right. That is the trap.
decision: Marisol is in the left glass and you need the door. How do you get out?

options.text: Far hand to the handle, look in the glass, then open a crack and look again
options.result: Right hand across. Your torso turns. The glass has her. You wait. She passes with three feet of ice and does not look at you. You open after. The crate follows. Nobody on the ice had to choose between a door and a wheel.

options.text: Open it now — she has time to stop on ice
options.result: The door occupies her line. Ice does not let her stop. The bar-end takes the steel and she goes down. Quiet lot, loud metal. She gets up. You will see her in every glass for a week.

options.text: Crack the window and tell her to go around
options.result: She cannot hear you through wind and ice and a moving bike. She is already in the door when you finish the sentence. Talking is not a look.

options.text: Get out the passenger side to avoid her entirely
options.result: The crates are in the way. You climb. The passenger door opens into a cart corral on ice. You fall. She passes a car that is now a spectacle. You avoided a door zone by inventing a worse one.

debrief: The door zone is the strip a bicyclist dies in. Far hand turns your body toward the mirror, then look, then open. You saved three feet of ice for her wheel.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Door zone: look before open; far-hand reach (4.6 bike-lanes body). Skill six is a soft PSDP home.

title: Search the Edges Again
hook: School zone, heavy rain. The painted 20 is a black river.
scene: Heavy rain at dawn, a Kent school zone you have already used in better weather. The lamps are flashing again. The painted 20 is a black river. You know the number. Knowing is not looking. A parked car on the right has its door an inch off latched — you will not see that if your eyes stay in the middle of the empty yard. Looking ahead is the next twelve seconds of hedge, bumper, glass, lamp, repeat. The insulin is the last crate. The Menace wants to be done. Done is how people skip the search they already passed on a quiz.
decision: You have done this zone before. Where are your eyes for the next twelve seconds?

options.text: Middle of the empty yard — you already know nothing uses it
options.result: The door opens. Not Marisol. A volunteer getting a tarp. You find him with the plow's right corner and a sound like a drum in the rain. You knew the 20. You did not look at the door.

options.text: Hedge, parked doors, crosswalk, lamps, then the middle, then again
options.result: Left hedge. Right bumpers. The inch-open door is a door. You cover and miss it. The crosswalk is empty and you treat it like it is not. The lamps fall behind you. The last crate stays a crate. That is looking ahead after you already knew the answer.

options.text: Watch the speedo until it sits on 20, then you are legal
options.result: The number is perfect. The door is still a door. Legal and looking are not the same exam. You pass the first and fail the second with a corner of pink steel.

options.text: Follow the wet tracks of whoever came through last so you do not have to search
options.result: The tracks go through a puddle that hides a curb. You take it. The person ahead was not searching either. Their line is not a plan.

debrief: Looking ahead is a loop you run every block. Search the edges — parked doors, hedges, the crosswalk — even in a zone you already passed. Ali searches the edges she already knew.

source.psdp_skill: Skill six: looking ahead
source.teaching_target: Skill six looking-ahead search loop; school zone is setting, not lesson. dol n/a: 4.17 would cite the rule option (c) marks wrong.

title: Clip, Tug, Then Roll
hook: The belt is off. Clip it before you roll.
scene: Fog at midday at the edge of The Grid. Cones ending. Central is next — a Kent street, four lanes, not this quiet paint. You reach for the shifter and the belt is not there. It was, this morning. It is not now. Deac would not start a log line without it. The Menace's cheap aftermarket belt is a pain in the mesh. That is not a reason to leave it off. You can hear the shelter radio from here. Clip it before you roll onto Central.
decision: The belt is off and The Grid is ending. What happens before you take the next street?

options.text: Go — you will clip it at the next stop, and the fog is already eating time
options.result: You do not get a next stop. A volunteer comes out of the fog already braking. You dump yours. The cheap belt that was not on does not hold. The game does not show the rest. It does not have to.

options.text: Clip it at rolling speed so you do not lose the gap
options.result: One hand off, eyes in your lap, torn-up lip under the tires. You miss the latch. The volunteer is already in your fog. You correct the wheel late. The belt never clicked.

options.text: Stop fully off the travel lane, clip, tug the belt, then roll
options.result: You refuse the last-second. Gravel. Click. Tug. The aftermarket latch takes. You roll out of the fog with a belt on and The Grid behind you. Central is the next place. You still have a body in the seat to hand it to.

options.text: Loop it over your shoulder without the latch so at least it looks done
options.result: The sash does no work when the first hard brake arrives. The webbing slides through. You are out of the seat the cheap belt was supposed to keep. The latch was the whole point.

debrief: Belt on, latched, tugged, before the vehicle moves. Not at the next stop. Not over the shoulder. Clip it, tug it, then roll.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Fasten and tug the seat belt before moving; a belt over the shoulder that is not latched is not a belt.

title: Drive Around the Block
hook: Willis dead-ends into a berm. Reverse lights do the talking.
scene: Willis dead-ends into a berm somebody pushed up and never came back for. The insulin still has forty minutes of cold, and the reroute is behind you. Houses on both sides, driveways every fifty feet. Gracie is up on the dash. Reverse lights are the brightest thing this car makes. Every second of backing is a second the mirrors are doing the work your eyes should be doing.
decision: You have to reverse direction. How?

options.text: Drive the block — right at the corner, right again, back onto Willis facing out
options.result: Four right turns, no reverse gear, no white lights. You come back onto Willis pointed out, the berm behind you. It cost ninety seconds and it cost nothing else.

options.text: U-turn right here — the street is empty and it takes four seconds
options.result: You swing it and the nose comes around across a double yellow you did not look down at. It works. It also would not have, three feet later, where the road narrows and the drainage grate sits. The yellow was there the whole time.

options.text: Back into the nearest driveway and come out the other way
options.result: It works, and it takes you twenty feet of reverse with the white lights on and the mirrors doing all of it. Not wrong. Just more backing than the corner would have cost you, on a street where backing is the expensive thing.

options.text: Three-point turn in the lane — forward, reverse, forward
options.result: You end up crosswise in a residential lane with the nose in one gutter and the tail in the other, reverse lights on, going nowhere for a beat and a half. Anything coming around the corner arrives at a car that is a wall.

debrief: The safest way to turn around is to drive around the block. Less backing is always better — backing is slower and blinder. Ali drives the block and never puts it in reverse.

source.psdp_skill: Skill seven: turning around
source.teaching_target: Around-the-block turnaround (Skill seven). KEEP 4.14 soft REVIEW — Turning body is intersections, not turnarounds.

title: The Driveway You Can See
hook: The corner is gone. Four driveways. Thirty-eight of cold.
scene: The corner is gone too — a transformer came down across it in the night and the wires are still on the pole. No block to drive around. Four driveways in reach: one across the street, one thirty feet up on your side against a blind hedge, one on your side with clean sight down Willis, one behind you past the crest. The pack still has thirty-eight minutes of cold.
decision: No block. You are backing into a driveway. Which one?

options.text: Your side, the one with clear sight down Willis — signal, check behind, back in
options.result: You pull just past it, blinker on, nothing behind you, and reverse in with two hundred feet of empty road in the mirror the whole time. Shift to drive, check both ways, and roll out pointed the right direction.

options.text: The one across the street — it is the widest and the apron is flat
options.result: Backing into it means dragging the car across the oncoming lane and sitting in it, sideways, blind to the crest. The apron is flat and it does not matter. You are a gate across the only road.

options.text: The near one at thirty feet — closest, least time exposed
options.result: The hedge eats Willis at about eighty feet. You are in reverse with a sightline shorter than your stopping distance, and the first thing you would know about anything coming is the sound of it.

options.text: Past the crest behind you — the driveway there is long and straight
options.result: You reverse up and over the crest to reach it, which means backing blind over the one piece of road you cannot see the far side of. The driveway is fine. Everything before the driveway is not.

debrief: A two-point turn backs into a driveway on the same side of the street as your car, at a spot with at least two hundred feet of visible road ahead. Pull just past it, signal, confirm nothing is behind you, then reverse. Stop and check both ways before you pull out.

source.psdp_skill: Skill seven: turning around
source.teaching_target: Two-point turn (Skill seven). KEEP 4.14 soft REVIEW — no DOL turnaround child; do not mint one.

title: Into the Dash
hook: Hard stop. Something orange hits the dash.
scene: A stop comes up faster than the street said it would — a kid on a bike, or a door, or a light that was yellow when you looked last. You stand on the pedal. You never buckled in at the lot and you're about to find out what that costs. Gracie leaves the seat and hits the cracked pink dash with a sound that is small and wrong. She is not hurt. You are not sure of that for a second. The belt is still hanging by the pillar where you left it.
decision: Gracie is on the dash and the street is still moving around you. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the stop. Put a hand on her. Buckle yourself before you roll again.
options.result: You stay stopped. You put a hand on her until she settles back onto the seat. Then you click the belt you skipped at the lot. The street can wait for that.

options.text: Roll through — she landed, keep moving
options.result: You keep rolling. She is still finding the seat. The next stop will be the same story because the belt is still hanging.

options.text: Pull over and put her in the carrier
options.result: You pull over. She will not stay in the carrier any more than she did at the lot. You spend the stop on a fight you already lost, and you are still unbuckled.
