options.text: Yell at her to stay on the seat
options.result: Your voice fills the cab. She flinches. The belt is still not on you. The street got louder for nothing.

debrief: The belt was yours at the lot. A hard stop in the Grid is where that bill comes due.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Physical debt from I-003. Hard stop puts Gracie on the dash. Scene names the lot belt in the clause.

title: Your Wheel
hook: Deac has the wheel.
scene: Central at morning, two lanes, wet paint. You are in the jump seat. Deac has the wheel and the thermos and the log. He will sweep the glass, hold the lane, then take one merge late on purpose so you can watch what that costs. He talks while he drives. You do not touch the wheel until he says so.
debrief: You saw the merge you do not take. He spent another man's margin to keep his. Deac hands you the wheel.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Demonstrate-first: sweep, hold right, never take a late merge; consequence is a horn and a man who had to lift.

title: Mya Has the Glass
hook: Mya is on the dash.
scene: The Ledger is parked at the curb on Central at dawn, engine still, key in. The cab is a high seat and a thermos empty since yesterday. Mya is a brown mackerel loaf on the dash — dark stripe, green eyes. The clipboard sits on the doghouse between the seats, next to the thermos. Amber vest, taped at the shoulder. Ali is still in the jump seat from the ride-along. Your hands rest on the wheel. The cluster reads zero. You have not rolled yet.
debrief: High seat, empty thermos, clipboard on the doghouse between the seats, next to the thermos. Parked: the cluster reads zero. Mya is a loaf on the dash. The big west-coast mirror on his door is how this bus sees the right once you roll.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Establish the Ledger cab parked: cluster at 0, Mya on the dash, clipboard on the doghouse, oversize door mirrors.

title: Stay Right Until You Pass
hook: Slow car ahead. The left is empty.
scene: Rain on a Kent morning, Central Avenue, two lanes south. You are in the right. A primer sedan is doing twenty-eight in that same lane, ahead of the Ledger. The left is open asphalt. The schedule wants past him. Sitting in the left after you pass is how a bus becomes the next twenty-eight.
decision: The slow car is in your lane and the left is clear. What do you do?

options.text: Hold the right and sit behind him until he notices
options.result: You match his twenty-eight. The schedule bleeds. The left stays empty while you teach him nothing. Central learns the Ledger will wait.

options.text: Signal, take the left, clear him, signal, come back right
options.result: Amber crawls. You take the left, pass, cancel, recover. He stays twenty-eight in the right. You did not become the next camper. The left stayed a tool.

options.text: Straddle both — the Ledger is wide enough that he will yield
options.result: You occupy the skip-dash. He brakes. Nobody can pass you, including you. Two lanes become one because you wanted both.

options.text: Move left, clear him, and stay in the left — through traffic can live here
options.result: You pass once and become the new slow in the passing lane. Everyone who needed the left now needs you. Keep-right did not expire because you passed once.

debrief: When several lanes run the same way, drive in the right lane and use the left to pass. You saved the left as a tool by coming back.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Drive in the right lane. Use the left lane to pass slower traffic, then return to the right.

title: Sweep Before You Change
hook: Cones shut the right. You need left.
scene: Midday fog, work zone. Cones pinch the right lane shut, so you need the left. On this bus the look that matters is the big side mirror on the left door, then over your left shoulder. Fog on the windshield is why one glance is not enough.
decision: You need the left lane. What do you look at, and in what order?

options.text: Glance left once and go — the right is cones so the left must be empty
options.result: You take the left on one look. A motorcycle you never owned is in the blind spot the side mirror would have shown. He stands on it. You stand on it. The cones get a new story.

options.text: Watch the opening until it is yours, then check the glass as you commit
options.result: The opening closes while your eyes are in it. You drift. A cone kisses the side of the bus. The sweep you skipped was the only thing that would have told you the gap was already gone.

options.text: Left glass, left door mirror, over the left shoulder, then the gap
options.result: You run the sweep. The side mirror has a motorcycle in it that a glance at the windshield missed. You wait one more gap. When you take it, he is already past you.

options.text: Trust the side mirror alone — skip the shoulder
options.result: The side mirror shrinks a pickup into a toy. You take the gap on a toy. He is a wall. You put the Ledger's shoulder in his.

debrief: The Ledger has blind spots you cannot see unless you sweep them. Left glass, left door mirror, shoulder, then the gap. Deac runs that sweep every time the Ledger changes lanes.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Mirror + OTS before lane change. dol n/a: Skill nine look procedure carries it; not 5.5 Focus.

title: The Van You Cannot See
hook: His nose is just in the window. The seat misses him.
scene: Clear cold afternoon on West Valley. You already signaled left. Look right: the door mirror is empty of him. At the edge of the passenger window, the faintest bite of a white van's nose — parallel, same way, no lamps. That is all the seat gets. The rest of him is in the blind spot beside the box. Nudge right to make the left feel bigger and you hit him. Take the left anyway and he can stay on the box and come with you.
decision: You can barely see his nose in the right window. What do you do?

options.text: Cancel, hold the lane, let him show or fall back, then take a clean gap
options.result: You kill the blinker and hold. He appears in the right door glass a second later, then drops. The next gap is empty. You take it without writing him into the steel.

options.text: Finish the left — he is on the right, so the left is empty
options.result: You take the left anyway. He was tucked on the right of the box, and he stays there as you move. Now you are both in the new lane and you still cannot see him. Steel on steel.

options.text: Drift right first to square up, then take the left
options.result: You drift right to get a better look. He is already in that space. The side of the bus takes the van.

options.text: Tap the horn so he knows to drop back
options.result: The horn on Central. He flinches into you. You both stop in a live lane. Everything behind has to lift.

debrief: A sliver of nose in the window is still a van in the blind spot. Kill the blinker, hold, then take a gap you have swept. Wait until he is a van you can see.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Blind-spot sliver: cancel, hold, then sweep. Skill nine look primary; 5.2 Space is weak REVIEW only.

title: A Hundred Feet of Amber
hook: Amber letters crawl. The column has not seen you yet.
scene: Wind at dusk on 167, a three-vehicle stack you did not ask for. You need the left in a hundred feet. Radios are trash. The Ledger talks with amber — your sign, your stalk. If you wink the stalk at the last second, the box behind you will eat your rear doors.
decision: You need the left in a hundred feet. How do you tell the column?

options.text: Move first, then signal — they will see the bus and understand
options.result: You start the change. The box behind had no sentence. He stands on it. You stand on it. The sign stays dark. You spent his brakes to keep your schedule.

options.text: Flash the highs twice — faster than a blinker and they cannot miss it
options.result: The flash hits his glass and comes back. He thinks you are warning him of something ahead. He slows in your gap. You still have not said left.

options.text: Leave the sign dark and use the stalk at the last skip-dash
options.result: The stalk talks for ten feet. He is already in your door. Late is the same as silent on a bus this long.

options.text: Sign left, stalk on, hold a hundred feet, then take a swept gap
options.result: Amber crawls LEFT. The stalk agrees. You hold the lane until the box lifts. The gap you take is one he already gave you. That is a sentence.

debrief: Signal a hundred feet before you move. The destination sign is the same sentence for a column that cannot hear you. Late amber still hits them as a surprise.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Signal at least 100 feet before a lane change; give the column time to answer.

title: Count the Gap First
hook: The gap looks big enough. Count it anyway.
scene: Heavy rain at night on Meeker. Ahead of you a pickup, then a gap, then a dark SUV, both going your way. The opening looks Ledger-shaped. Your foot agrees. The ride-along is still in your hands: if you cannot count it, keep waiting. The thermos does not argue. The schedule does.
decision: A gap just opened between them. Do you take it?

options.text: Hold until you can count a full Ledger plus a breath, then take it
options.result: You wait. The SUV closes what looked like a gap. The next opening is longer. You count it, take it, and nobody has to lift. Late on the log. Alive in the lane.

options.text: Take it now — rain makes people generous and the pickup already lifted
options.result: You put the nose in. The SUV did not lift. You make him. Horn, spray, the Ledger's shoulder in his. That was the late merge you already watched.

options.text: Nose in and force the zipper — they will make room for a bus
options.result: You write your length into a gap that was a car. He stands on it. You stand on it. Two lanes become one argument.

options.text: Match the pickup's speed and wait for him to wave you through
options.result: He never waves. You sit on his bumper in the rain until the light. You did not count a gap. You waited for permission Central does not give.

debrief: Merge only into a gap you can count — your length, plus room so nobody has to swerve or stand on it. You missed a wreck by waiting one extra breath.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: 5.3 Merging (not 5.2): accept only a gap where others need not swerve, slow, or stop.

title: Broken White, Solid White
hook: Solid white fences the diamond on the left.
scene: Overcast on a divided highway. Three lanes this way. A diamond sits in the leftmost lane against the median, fenced from the general lanes by solid white pavement marking. You are in the general lane immediately right of that paint, in a stack. Skip-dashes between general lanes are a legal change if the gap is real. The solid is not. The Ledger wants out. The paint decides, not the want.
decision: You want out of this stack. Which paint do you cross?

options.text: Cross the solid white into the diamond — it is empty and faster
options.result: You take the diamond. The sign said two. You are one and a bus. A trooper remnant in a dark cap sits in the next ramp. You just wrote a restricted lane onto the log.

options.text: Straddle the broken white until someone makes a gap
options.result: You occupy the dash. Both lanes lose you. The stack behind has to guess which space you want. Nobody guesses right.

options.text: Wait for a gap and cross only the broken white. Leave the solid alone
options.result: You hold. A gap opens on the broken side. You take it, cancel, and leave the diamond to the people who paid for it. The paint stayed a sentence.

options.text: Use the solid as a shoulder to let the stack pass, then come back
options.result: The solid never offered you a shoulder. You put a bus on the rumble. Snow and a drain. The stack passes you as a wreck.

debrief: Broken white between same-direction lanes may be crossed to change lanes. Solid white marks an edge or a restricted lane. Deac leaves the diamond to the people who paid for it.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Cross broken white to change lanes; do not cross solid white pavement marking into a restricted lane.

title: Hollis on Your Bumper
hook: Hollis fills the left door glass. Open your front gap.
scene: Ice on a Kent morning, 256th doing the speed of Central. Hollis is in the lifted truck again, filling the left door mirror, close enough that his plow is a suggestion. If you brake for the light you cannot see yet, he writes you into the doghouse between the seats. The six-second habit from the Grid still works. You just have to spend it ahead, not behind.
decision: Hollis is on your bumper at speed. What do you change?

options.text: Brake-check him once so he finds a legal following distance
options.result: You tap. He does not have ice tires. He has a lift and a wish. His plow kisses your rear doors. Central hears it.

options.text: Open your own front gap and hold speed so you can roll instead of stand on it
options.result: You lift a breath off the truck ahead. The next light goes yellow. You roll it out instead of planting. Hollis has to lift with you or eat you. He lifts. You never touched him.

options.text: Move left now and let him have this lane
options.result: You take a gap you did not sweep because he is loud. A sedan is in the left blind spot. You make three problems out of one bumper.

options.text: Match him and close the front — if you are a box he cannot hit you as hard
options.result: You close the front. The light you could not see is red. You and Hollis and the truck ahead become one piece of ice.

debrief: When someone tailgates, open YOUR gap ahead so you can roll instead of plant. You cannot fix his bumper. Hold your own front gap and refuse the chain.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: If tailgated, increase the gap ahead so you can brake gradually; do not brake-check.

title: The Panel Again
hook: Same white van. Same blind spot. He remembered you.
scene: Clear cold afternoon on West Valley, same paint, same sun angle. The white panel van is in the right-side blind spot again — the room beside the bus — closer, lamps still off. Last time you drifted into him. This time he is already hugging the Ledger like a grudge. The blinker wants left. The side mirror is honest. He already knows this move.
decision: The van is in the right-side blind spot and you still need left. What do you do with the debt?

options.text: Hold, let him declare, and take a gap you have swept twice
options.result: You hold. He finally shows a lamp and drops back. The gap you take is empty. He does not get a second kiss of steel. That is the apology.

options.text: Finish the left fast so he cannot stay on your flank
options.result: You snatch the left. He comes with you again. Same steel, same afternoon. He was waiting for the same move.

options.text: Drift right and pin him to the curb so he cannot follow
options.result: You use the bus as a wall. He has nowhere. The curb takes his wheel. You collected the debt with his quarter panel.

options.text: Stop in the lane and wait until he goes around
options.result: You plant a bus on West Valley. He goes around into the left you wanted. Everyone behind you gets a new problem.

debrief: A miss in the right-side blind spot comes back on the same street. Sweep, hold, then move. The same van is still there, lamps still off, waiting for the same drift.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Hold until right blind is empty, then move. Skill nine look primary; 5.2 Space weak REVIEW (III-005 debt).

variation.forced: location+weather+time match III-005 callback street

title: See His Mirrors or Leave
hook: You're beside his trailer. He can't see you here.
scene: Overcast midday on 167. A rogue semi with no door marks and a dirty number that used to be ninety is in the right lane. You are in the left, beside the rear half of his trailer. Old Ninety. The big west-coast mirrors on his doors sit far ahead on the cab. If you cannot see those mirrors, he cannot see you. The schedule wants you past him. You are in the place a truck cannot see.
decision: You are coming up on Old Ninety's left rear quarter. Where do you sit?

options.text: Hold beside the trailer — his length is a windbreak and the left is empty
options.result: You cruise the no-zone. He starts a right that needs your lane. You are the car in the statistic. He never had you in the glass.

options.text: Tuck under his tail — if you cannot see him he cannot hit you
options.result: You sit in the gap behind a loaded trailer. He cannot see you and he cannot stop for you. The next brake is yours.

options.text: Pass on the shoulder — the rumble is safer than his left
options.result: The shoulder is a drain and a sign post. You put a bus in the junk. He never knew you tried.

options.text: Drop back until both his mirrors show you, or commit the pass and clear
options.result: You fall back until two dirty west-coast mirrors on his doors hold a Ledger. Then you pass once, all the way, and you do not linger. He keeps his blind spots. You keep your steel.

debrief: If you cannot see a truck's mirrors, the driver cannot see you. Do not live beside the trailer. You missed being the car in his turn.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Stay out of a truck's blind zones; if you cannot see the driver's mirrors, you are invisible.

title: Do Not Live Beside
hook: The no-zones are drawn on the asphalt. Do not sit in them.
scene: Rain at dusk, still 167, the same trailer length painted in your head. Passing a truck takes the whole trailer, then the cab, then room to come back. If you linger at the drive axle you are in a space he uses to turn. The Ledger knows this from the other side. Tonight you are the car.
decision: You have started a pass on a trailer. When are you done?

options.text: When your nose is past his — that is enough to claim the lane
options.result: You recover early. Your rear doors are still at his drive axle. He starts the right he signaled a mile ago. You are the lingering car.

options.text: When you see his whole front in your glass and the bus is clear, then recover
options.result: You stay in the pass until the trailer is a trailer in the glass, not a wall at your shoulder. You recover once. He keeps his turn. You keep your doors.

options.text: Match his speed beside the cab so he sees you and can wave you past
options.result: You become a passenger on his left. He cannot wave a bus through a no-zone. He needs that space to live.

options.text: Cut in as soon as you see pavement in front of him — leave him a car length
options.result: You give a loaded trailer a car length at highway speed. He cannot stop. You just borrowed his stopping distance.

debrief: Do not linger beside a truck. Pass, then recover only when the whole front of his vehicle is in your mirror and you have left him stopping room. Deac would not live beside a trailer he used to drive.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Never linger beside a large vehicle; complete the pass and leave stopping room before merging back.

title: Twenty-Six, None Preventable
hook: Twenty-six years. The schedule is louder now.
scene: Fog on a downtown ramp at night, the Ledger idling in a legal pocket. Glasses on a cord. Clipboard on the thigh. Twenty-six years and he never wrote a preventable. The schedule used to be a promise to the people in the back. Now it is a number that wants the late gap you already refused. The thermos is still empty. That is the cost of the number.
debrief: Deac's record is a habit he paid for in empty thermoses. The schedule still matters. It does not get to spend someone else's margin. Two clean stops reset him. Leave the late gap for someone else's log.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Deac beat: twenty-six years without a preventable; the schedule is not permission to take a late gap.

title: Arrow, Then Circle
hook: The arrow dies. The circle is still green.
scene: Clear cold dawn, high seat, a left-turn pocket on Central. A green arrow has been feeding you. It dies. The circular green stays. Oncoming still has a path. The Ledger's nose is already in the intersection because you trusted the arrow. The yellow line you want is still across a live lane.
decision: The arrow is gone and the circle is green. Do you finish the left?

options.text: Go now — you were in the intersection on the arrow, so you own it
options.result: You take the circular green as if the arrow were still up. Oncoming is a pair of lamps you did not yield to. You make them lift. The pocket never promised you that turn.

options.text: Sit in the pocket until another arrow — circular green is a trap
options.result: You become a bus in a pocket through two cycles. The stack behind you starts using the through lanes. You taught the light that Deac does not know the difference.

options.text: Yield to oncoming, then take the closest lane right of their yellow when it is clear
options.result: You wait. Oncoming clears. You steer to the first lane right of their yellow, not the far one. The arrow was a gift. The circle is a yield.

options.text: Swing wide into the far lane so you are out of oncoming's way faster
options.result: You exit into the far lane. A through car already owns it. You traded a yield for a sideswipe.

debrief: A green arrow means the other direction is stopped for you. A circular green means yield, then finish in the closest lane to the right of the yellow. The arrow going dark is the yield starting.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part two
source.teaching_target: Protected left on a green arrow; permissive circular green requires a yield, then the nearest lane right of the yellow.

title: The Center Lane Turns Only
hook: The pocket is for turns. The stack wants a pass.
scene: Wind on a Kent morning. A two-way left-turn lane down the middle, arrows both ways, the same idea as the Grid's dead-van pocket except this one is legal if you are actually turning. A primer sedan is using it as a travel lane to beat the light. Your left is coming up in two blocks. The pocket will take you. It will not take you for a mile.
decision: The two-way pocket is empty for a long stretch. How do you use it?

options.text: Enter only when you are ready to turn, and do not travel farther than you need
options.result: You wait until the turn is real. You take the pocket for a short bite, yield to the other direction, and finish. The sedan is still touring it like a lane when oncoming wants it.

options.text: Use it as a passing lane — that is what the dashes are for
options.result: You pass in a lane that belongs to both directions. Oncoming enters it to turn. Two noses, one paint. The dashes never meant pass.

options.text: Ride it for the next mile so you are already in position at every left
options.result: You travel the center. Three driveways and a car coming the other way all have a claim. Three hundred feet was the limit. You spent it like a highway.

options.text: Straddle the yellow and the pocket so nobody can surprise you
options.result: You occupy two lanes. Through traffic has to guess. The pocket is no longer a pocket. It is a problem with your name on it.

debrief: A two-way left-turn lane is for turning. Enter it to turn, watch the other direction, and do not tour it. You saved a head-on in paint that belongs to both ways.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part two
source.teaching_target: Use a two-way left-turn lane only to turn; do not travel or pass in it.

title: The Hood Line Walks
hook: The hood line walks toward the rumble. Your eyes were gone.
scene: Overcast afternoon, a long straight on 167, nothing to do with your hands but hold. The thermos is empty. The hood line has walked an inch toward the rumble and you did not tell it to. That is the Drift with a lowercase d until you name it. A clean stop would reset it. There is no legal shoulder that will not become a story. The timeout is the walk.
decision: The hood line is walking and you felt the skip. What do you do?

options.text: Shake it off and hold speed — the straight will end and you will be fine
options.result: You argue with a nervous system. The walk becomes a tire on the rumble. The stack behind you gets a new shape of bus.

options.text: Crack a window and talk — conversation is as good as a stop
options.result: You talk to an empty jump seat. The walk continues. Conversation does not put sleep back in your eyes. The rumble finds you anyway.

options.text: Speed up so the air keeps you honest
options.result: You add speed to a microsleep. The Drift does not care about your schedule. It cares that you are still moving.

options.text: Signal, find a legal pad, key off, twenty minutes. The log can wait.
options.result: You take the next ramp pad, hazards, key off. Twenty minutes with the key off. The hood line is a hood line when you start again. Two clean stops reset him. This is one.

debrief: Lane drift, heavy eyes, missing a stretch of road — pull off and rest. Deac owes the log a stop, not another mile.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Treat lane drift and a missing stretch of road as fatigue; stop and rest rather than push through.

title: The Side Mirror Points Up
hook: The right side mirror is pointing at the sky.
scene: Heavy rain at dusk in a work zone. A cone you did not own kissed the right mirror arm. The side mirror now looks at the sky. Mya is boxed on the doghouse between the seats. The Ledger just lost the look at its right. You can keep rolling on a guess or you can make the glass tell the truth again.
decision: The right side mirror is pointed at the weather. What do you do?

options.text: Keep rolling — you still have the left door mirror and the shoulder check
options.result: You guess the right-side blind spot. A work van is in it. You find him with the side of the bus. The left door mirror never had that angle.

options.text: Cover the dead glass with your hand so it stops lying
options.result: You drive one-handed in a work zone. The lie is gone. So is a hand. The next cone is closer than your remaining glass.

options.text: Hazards, legal pad, reset the arm until the side mirror sees the lane again
options.result: You put the bus on a pad and put the glass back on the lane. Two minutes in the rain. The right-side blind spot returns as a picture. You do not buy a sideswipe with a schedule.

options.text: Switch to the left only and refuse all right-side changes
options.result: The next merge is a right. You refuse it and become a rolling roadblock in a closed pattern. The work crew has to wave you through a lie you would not fix.

debrief: A mirror that does not see the lane is a maintenance problem. Guessing the right-side blind spot is how you collect a van. Stop and set the arm before you take another gap.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: A knocked side mirror must be reset before you keep changing lanes; do not drive on a blind right.

title: The Whole Front in Glass
hook: You are alongside. The pass still has work.
scene: Rain at night on Central, a box doing thirty in the right. You are in the left, mid-pass, the Ledger's nose past his cab. Recovering now would put your rear doors in his windshield. See the whole front in the glass, then come back. A bus this long stays humble about when a pass is done.
decision: Your nose is past him. When do you come back?

options.text: Now — you are ahead, and the right is yours again
options.result: You recover on a guess. His windshield fills with your rear doors. He stands on it. You taught him that a pass is a suggestion.

options.text: When his whole front is in your glass and the bus is clear, then signal and recover
options.result: You wait until the box is a box in the mirror, not a wall at your hip. You signal, come back, cancel. He never had to lift. That is a finished pass.

options.text: Stay in the left after you pass — through traffic can live here
options.result: You become the new slow in the passing lane. Everyone who needed the left now needs you. Keep-right did not expire because you passed once.

options.text: Cut in tight to teach him thirty is too slow
options.result: You give him a breath of asphalt at night in the rain. A box cannot stop on a breath. You spent his margin to make a point.

debrief: Finish the pass. Recover only when the passed vehicle's whole front is in your mirror and you are clear. Then get out of the left. The box should already be a box in the glass.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part two
source.teaching_target: Pass-complete / lane-position space: recover when full front is in the mirror. KEEP 5.2 Space — not III-004 mirror-sweep n/a.

title: The Sign Talks First
hook: The sign lights SLOW. Someone is in your doors.
scene: Snow at deep night, a volunteer box on your bumper who joined without asking. You need to dump speed for a dead pickup in the right. The stalk will talk to him late. The destination sign talks to a column. Radios are still trash. Amber is the language. If you only use the brake lamps, he eats your rear doors and you invent passengers.
decision: You need to slow and the volunteer is tight. How do you tell him?

options.text: Sign SLOW, left arm down if the lamps are buried, then lift off
options.result: Amber crawls SLOW. Your left arm goes out and down for the man who cannot see a sign through snow. He lifts. You dump speed without writing him into the doors. The pickup stays a pickup.

options.text: Stand on the brakes — the lamps are the sentence
options.result: The lamps dump. He does not. Your rear doors become his windshield. You just made passengers out of a volunteer and a schedule.

options.text: Wave him around on the left before you slow
options.result: You wave a stranger into a snow lane you have not swept. He goes. The dead pickup was not the only object. You spent him.

options.text: Leave the sign dark so you do not draw the Quiet, and hope he reads the stalk
options.result: The stalk talks for ten feet of snow. He never had a sentence. Hoping he reads a blinker is how you invent passengers.

debrief: Tell the column before you dump speed. The destination sign is the sentence; the left arm down is the backup when snow buries the lamps. You saved the volunteer a face full of your doors.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Communicate a slow-down to following traffic with the sign and, if needed, the left-arm-down signal.

variation.forced: live still cards/takes/III-019-c-take-2.png (art-review pick; was live≠pick)

title: The Straight Again
hook: The same straight comes back.
scene: Overcast afternoon on 167, the same long straight. Last time your eyes left it — sleep or a screen, the mile does not care. This time the right rear tires are already on the rumble and the skip-dash is a smear. The thermos is still empty. A pad is coming up on the right, legal, ugly, enough. The Drift does not give second warnings. It gives the same mile twice.
decision: The right rear tires are on the rumble again. What do you do with the second chance?

options.text: Hold the wheel harder and finish the straight — you know it now
options.result: Knowing the mile does not put sleep in your eyes. You walk it into the rumble for real. The stack behind you writes a new shape.

options.text: Open a window and slap the dash until the line comes back
options.result: You make noise in a tired cab. The line does not come back. Mya would have, if she were here. Slapping the dash does not put sleep in your eyes.

options.text: Take the pad. Hazards. Key off. Twenty minutes you already owed.
options.result: You take the ugly pad. Key off. The log waits. When you start again the hood line is a hood line. That is the only apology the straight accepts.

options.text: Hand the wheel to whoever is in the jump — anyone awake is better
options.result: The jump is empty. You reach for a person who is not there and the rumble takes the rest.

debrief: The same straight comes back when you push through. Deac already owed this pad twenty minutes.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: A repeated lane-drift on the same stretch means stop and rest; do not tough out a second microsleep.

variation.forced: location+weather+time match III-016 callback stretch

title: Reyna Off-Route
hook: A transit box signals out. She is not on the shelter run.
scene: Clear cold morning, downtown edge, a transit box pulling off a stop with its stalk already talking. Reyna is in a different seat today — not Bus 12, a city coach, off the shelter route, still on time. The law is the same: if she has signaled and she is coming back, you yield. The Ledger can eat a bus. The schedule cannot eat Reyna.
decision: She has signaled and the coach is coming back onto your lane. What do you do?

options.text: Hold speed — she can wait, you are already in the through lane
options.result: You keep the lane she needs. She stands on it or she clips you. She stands. You taught a transit driver that through traffic does not yield.

options.text: Pass her on the left before she commits — get it over with
options.result: You go for the left as her nose comes out. She is already in the lane. Two boxes, one gap. Downtown hears it.

options.text: Horn once so she knows you see her, then keep your speed
options.result: The horn on a cold downtown edge. She flinches and stops half out. You still did not give her the lane. You just announced the block.

options.text: Lift, give her the lane, and take her back once she is through
options.result: You lift. She takes the lane she already asked for. You roll in behind her. Two fingers off the wheel, not a wave. Off-route or not, she still runs on time.

debrief: Yield to a transit vehicle in your direction that has signaled and is pulling back on. The stop is her work. Leave her the lane she already asked for.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Yield to a transit bus in your direction that has signaled and is reentering the roadway.

title: Siren First
hook: Siren first, then lamps. Something wants the right.
scene: Rain at midday, stacked on Central. The siren arrives before the lamps — that is the order when you are in a bus. Officer Dunn is in a dark WSP remnant, lights finding the gaps, same heading, coming up the stack. The law is older than the quarantine: right, stop, wait. The Chorus would love your eyes on a screen right now. The siren is the screen.
decision: Emergency vehicle behind, siren live. What do you do?

options.text: Signal, move right, stop, wait until he is past, then reenter in order
options.result: You put the Ledger on the right and plant it. Dunn takes the gap you made. When his lamps are gone you signal and take your place in the stack. Nobody invented a new order.

options.text: Hold the left and speed up so he can have the right
options.result: You run from a siren. He needs the right, and you just filled the passing lane. The stack becomes a wall with your name on it.

options.text: Stop in your lane immediately — he can go around
options.result: You plant a bus in a live lane. He has to invent a path. The man behind you does not stop. Three vehicles, one siren, no right.

options.text: Check the tablet for which way he is going, then decide
options.result: Your eyes leave the glass. The siren is already beside you. You decide late. That was the timeout, and it was a look.

debrief: Siren or lamps: move right, stop, wait until the emergency vehicle is past, then reenter in the order you had. Eyes stay on the glass, not on a screen.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Pull to the right and stop for an emergency vehicle using lights or siren; reenter in original order.

title: Hold the General Lane
hook: The diamond is empty. The box in your lane is slow.
scene: Fog at dusk on 167. A box is doing thirty in the general lane. To the left, a diamond on the pavement and a solid white fence, empty and fast. A bus may travel in that lane when the signs say so. What you cannot do is cross the solid to dart in, pass one vehicle, and dart out. Broken white is where entry is even legal. That diamond is not a passing lane you invented.
decision: The diamond is empty and he is slow. Do you use it to pass?

options.text: Dart into the diamond, pass, come back before the next ramp
options.result: You use a carpool lane as a slingshot. Solid white means stay out through that stretch. The remnant in the cap does not care that you are a bus. You stole a pass from a lane that was never yours to dart through.

options.text: Hold the general lane. If you pass, pass in a general lane.
options.result: You stay. The diamond stays empty. When a general lane opens you take a real pass or you don't. The box stays at thirty. You stay legal.

options.text: Straddle the solid white until he notices and moves over
options.result: You occupy the fence. He never moves. Both lanes lose you. The diamond was never a shoulder and the solid was never an invitation.

options.text: Take the rumble on the right and go around him there
options.result: The rumble is a drain in the fog. You put a bus in the junk to avoid a rule. He never knew you tried.

debrief: 4.16: HOV is a diamond, occupancy on the signs, typically fenced by solid white. A bus may travel in it. Solid means do not cross that stretch; broken is where you may enter or exit. Do not dart through the diamond to pass one slow vehicle.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: HOV is not a passing lane. Solid white: do not cross into it on that stretch. Broken white: you may enter or exit. A qualifying bus may travel in HOV, not dart through it.

title: Slow for the Water
hook: Posted forty-five. Rain. The six seconds got longer.
scene: Rain at night on West Valley, posted forty-five, water in the wheel tracks. The Grid taught six seconds on a quiet street. At Central's speed the same seconds are more asphalt. A pickup ahead is doing the number on the sign. Your tires are doing a rumor. The Splitter loves the posted number. The road wants less.
decision: The sign says forty-five and the asphalt is a river. What speed do you keep?

options.text: Hold forty-five — posted is posted and the pickup is the proof
options.result: You match him. The next brake is a wish. The Ledger's right rear tires write a story in the standing water. Posted was the maximum. The water set a lower one.

options.text: Drop to twenty and become the new problem
options.result: You become a roadblock in a live lane. The pickup goes around you in the rain. You traded a hydroplane for a sideswipe you invited.

options.text: Lift off until the six-second gap is real again, even if that is under posted
options.result: You give the water the seconds. The pickup pulls away. You can still see his tires meet the road. When the rain eases you take the number back. The sign never asked you to float.

options.text: Move left and hold forty-five in the drier tracks
options.result: The left tracks are also a river. You added a lane change on ice-that-is-rain. The number did not get safer because you switched paint.

debrief: On wet asphalt, slow until your following time is real again. Deac would rather be late than float.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Reduce speed below posted on wet roads so following time stays usable; posted is a maximum.

title: What He Sees at the Edge
hook: Ice on the far right of the glass. He does not look.
scene: Ice, deep night, the Ledger parked in a legal pocket off Aurora Avenue. A smear of ice sits at the far right of the windshield — no lamps, no car, no face. Deac's eyes stay in the cage, on the empty lane. He names it under his breath so the jump seat can hear: the Drift. Looking is how the Chorus gets in. The clipboard is on his thigh. The thermos is empty. He does not turn his head.
debrief: The Drift is fatigue given a shape at the edge of the glass. He manages it with stops and a thermos, not with stares. Look at the lane, not the smear.

source.psdp_skill: n/a
source.teaching_target: Name the Drift as Deac's fatigue antagonist; do not stare at the presence at the edge of vision.

title: Use Both Lanes, Then Zipper
hook: Both lanes still run. The sign says the right will die.
scene: Overcast dawn, a work zone that ate the right in a quarter mile. Both lanes still move. The early-merge instinct wants the left now, to be polite, to be first. The zipper wants both lanes used until the merge paint, then one-for-one. You already took a late gap once on purpose so she could watch the cost. This is the legal late. Different sentence.
decision: The right dies ahead. When do you merge left?

options.text: Stay in the right until the merge paint, then take turns with the left
options.result: You use the lane until it ends. At the teeth you take one, give one. The stack is shorter than the polite line that started a mile early. The sign meant it.

options.text: Move left now so you are not the person who cuts at the end
options.result: You join the polite line. The right stays empty and angry. Someone late uses it and you resent them for doing the zipper. You taught the zone the wrong courtesy.

options.text: Straddle both until the last cone so nobody can beat you
options.result: You occupy two lanes in a work zone. Nobody zippers. You are the blockage the sign was trying to prevent.

options.text: Stop at the first warning sign and wait for a flagger to assign a lane
options.result: There is no flagger. You plant a bus at a sign. The zipper happens without you, around you, angry.

debrief: For a lane closure, use both lanes until the merge point, then take turns — the zipper. Early merging out of courtesy builds a longer line and a nastier end.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Zipper merge: stay in your lane until the designated merge, then alternate.

title: The Tablet Wakes
hook: The tablet wakes mid-change. The Chorus wants a look.
scene: Wind on a Kent morning, left stalk already on, gap half-taken. The aftermarket tablet on the doghouse between the seats lights up — a familiar voice, a map, a lie. II-009's cousin. Eyes off a Beetle was bad. Eyes off the Ledger mid-change is how you write a sedan into the big west-coast mirror on the door. The timeout is the look.
decision: The screen lights up in the middle of a lane change. Where do your eyes go?

options.text: Glance the screen — one second, then finish the change
options.result: One second is a blind spot. The sedan was in it. You find him with the arm. The Chorus got the look it wanted.

options.text: Thumb the screen off while you steer — you can do two things
options.result: You steer with a thumb on glass. The gap moves. The Ledger does not. Two things was the problem.

options.text: Finish by memory — you already swept, the screen can wait
options.result: Memory is a stale sweep. The blind spot changed. You take a gap that closed. The tablet keeps talking to nobody.

options.text: Cancel the change, hold the lane, ignore the screen, sweep again, then move
options.result: You kill the stalk and let the tablet die alone. The gap you take later is one you have seen. The Chorus does not get a vote mid-change.

debrief: A screen mid-maneuver is a look you cannot afford. Cancel, hold, finish the driving, then the glass. You missed a sedan by killing the stalk.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part one
source.teaching_target: Do not take eyes off the road to a screen during a lane change; cancel and complete the driving first.

title: The Right Rear Tire Is Soft
hook: The right rear tire is soft. Snow is already on the paint.
scene: Snow on Central this afternoon. The Ledger has been wandering a half-inch toward the rumble for the last mile and this time the wander is rubber — the right rear tire is soft and the tread on that tire is a rumor. Two thirty-seconds is the floor. You can keep rolling on a wish or you can put the bus on a pad and know. The schedule wants the next light. The tire wants air.
decision: The right rear tire is soft and the tread looks thin. What do you do?

options.text: Keep rolling — a rear tire can run soft and the snow is only starting
options.result: You argue with rubber. The wander becomes a slide at the next brake. A right rear tire that is soft in snow does not wait for the Drift to take the credit.

options.text: Hazards, legal pad, check tread and pressure before you take more snow
options.result: You put the bus on a pad. Tread is at the wear bars on the outer. Pressure is low. You air it from the can on the rack and you do not take the next hill on a wish. Late on the log. Rolling on purpose.

options.text: Kick it once and if it sounds hard enough, go
options.result: A kick sounds like a tire. It is still soft. The next curve writes the rest. The door sticker was the number you skipped.

options.text: Overfill it by eye from the can so it cannot go soft again
options.result: You guess high. The tire is a drum. Handling gets worse, not better. The door sticker was the number. You did not read it.

debrief: Tread under two thirty-seconds slides on wet and snow. Pressure is on the door sticker, not in your foot. Deac airs it from the can before he takes another hill.

title: The Pass That Gains Nothing
hook: The pass would gain a length. The left is a wish.
scene: Heavy rain at dusk, two lanes, a box doing the same number you are. The left is empty for a breath. A pass would put you one length ahead and back in the same rain. If it gains nothing, it is only risk. The schedule will not notice a length. The Quiet might notice the extra noise.
decision: The left is open and he is doing your speed. Do you pass?

options.text: Pass now — empty left is permission and the schedule likes motion
options.result: You take a pass that buys a length. Recovering, you write spray across his glass. He lifts. You are one length richer and louder. The light ahead makes you even again.

options.text: Sit on his bumper until he notices and moves over
options.result: You become Hollis with a bus. He does not move. You spend Central as a threat. Nothing is gained except an enemy.

options.text: Flash him once so he yields the right, then take it without a pass
options.result: The flash is a demand. He brakes. You almost eat a box you did not need to pass. Permission you invented.

options.text: Hold the right. Keep the gap. Let the empty left stay empty
options.result: You stay. He stays. The left stays a lane for someone who needs it. You arrive the same minute you would have. That is the thesis: do not spend a pass you cannot cash.

debrief: Do not pass just because the left is empty. Pass to turn, to clear a hazard, to exit — not to own a length. Hold the right if the pass buys you nothing.

source.psdp_skill: Skill nine: multi-lane roads – part two
source.teaching_target: Do not change lanes or pass unnecessarily; keep right and only pass when the pass does useful work.

title: The Core From Here

title: Cover the brake
hook: Foot off the gas. Heel down under the pad. Ball hovering over the brake, ready to press.
scene: Encore ride-along. Yuna drives. Ali sits the welded rear bench, out of this frame. Cover the brake before the light even thinks about yellow. Foot off the gas. Held. Not riding it.

title: One Pedal at a Time
hook: Left foot is for a clutch. That's it.
scene: You are in the Menace now. Yuna's car had two pedals. This floor has three: clutch on the left, brake in the middle, gas on the right. Both of your feet are on the painted floor, not on anything. The left foot only works a pedal if the car has a clutch. Everything else is the right foot, and only one of those pedals at a time. Two feet on two pedals is how you fight the car.
decision: Which feet work the pedals?

options.text: Left foot on the brake, right foot on the gas, so you can switch faster
options.result: You plant both. The pads and the engine fight. The Menace hops. The stack behind you stands on it. Two pedals at once is not faster. It is how you lose the front and the rear in the same second.

options.text: Right foot for gas and brake, one at a time. Left foot only on a clutch
options.result: Left foot stays on the floor unless you need the clutch. Right foot takes the gas or the brake, never both. Encore had two pedals. The Menace has three. The rule did not change — only whether a clutch exists.

options.text: Left foot covers the brake on every car, automatic or not
options.result: You drop the left foot on the brake because it feels ready. The lamps light. Someone behind dumps speed for a stop you did not mean. Left foot is not a brake foot. The only pedal it is allowed to touch is a clutch.

options.text: Rest the left foot on the clutch so you are always ready
options.result: You leave the left foot on the left pedal. The clutch is already a little in. The Menace smells like a slip. Ready is the floor. The pedal is a choice, not a shelf.

debrief: Left foot stays on the floor unless you need the clutch. Right foot does one pedal. You kept the Menace from fighting itself.

source.psdp_skill: Skill two: moving, steering, and stopping
source.teaching_target: Left foot works a pedal only on a manual (the clutch). Otherwise right foot only, and only one pedal at a time.

title: Cover the Brake
hook: Foot off the gas. Held over the brake.
scene: Rain at midday on a four-lane downtown street. Yuna is already gone. You have the Menace and the mesh back. A light ahead is still green. options.text: Stay on the gas — the light is still green and you will lose the gap
options.result: You hold the gas. He is already stopped. You stand on it late. The plow talks to his bumper. Rain carries the note down the block. Whatever made him dump speed now has you too.

options.text: Lift off the gas and hold your foot over the brake without pressing it yet
options.result: You lift. The foot waits over the pedal. He bottoms out. You are already covering, so the stop is a press, not a panic. No note. The reason he stopped is a person you can now see.

debrief: Cover the brake: foot off the gas, held over the pedal, not riding it. You bought the second you needed when the sedan stopped. Keep the foot ready, not planted.

source.psdp_skill: Skill ten: city driving – part one
source.teaching_target: Cover the brake in traffic: lift off the accelerator and hold the foot over the brake without riding the pedal.

title: Between the Parked
hook: Someone steps out between the parked cars.
scene: Overcast, wet two-lane off the Core. The Menace is already in the street. A figure is walking out from the gap between a parked van and a gray sedan — coat, jeans, both shoes in the paint. You have the paper on your side. The person is already in your lane. The plow is the only vote that counts.

options.text: Hold speed — they should wait, and you have the street
options.result: You keep the number. They finish the step. The plow and a coat occupy the same paint. You dump it late. They freeze. You freeze. The side street now has a story it did not need.

options.text: Honk so they step back between the cars

options.result: You lift and cover. They see the plow and finish across. You never argue the paper. The side street stays a side street. You roll when the gap is a gap again.

title: The Double Threat

The timeout is the pass.

title: Tracks in the Lane
hook: Tracks sit in your lane. The train cannot swerve.
scene: Wind at night on a downtown street that still carries light rail. Steel sits in the asphalt of your lane — two rails, wet, the groove that eats a tire. A train is a set of lamps coming up those rails, same way, no steering to give you. You can straddle, you can race, or you can leave the rail to the thing that cannot leave it. options.text: Straddle the rails and hold speed — your tires can take the groove
options.result: A tire finds the groove and follows it. The plow walks. You fight the wheel while the lamps grow. The train does not have a wheel to fight. You become a problem on its rail.

options.text: Beat the train through the next light — it has to stop anyway
options.result: You try to own a rail the train already owns. It does not stop for your light. You dump speed on steel. The lamps fill the mesh. You were never going to win that race.

options.text: Stop on the rails so the train has to deal with you first
options.result: You plant a Beetle on steel. The train cannot swerve. The operator has one move and it is late. You made a crossing out of a travel lane.

options.text: Take the empty transit lane — nothing is coming and you are through traffic
options.result: You take the diamond's cousin. A bus remnant is already committed. You write a Beetle into a lane that was never yours. The remnant has to lift. Downtown remembers the plow in the wrong paint.

title: The Bike in the Gap
hook: A motorcycle is already in the lane you wanted.
scene: Rain at morning on a four-lane downtown street. You already threw the left stalk. The left looks like a gap. In the left door glass a motorcycle is already there — low, same way, one lamp, a rider in a dark jacket, filling the space you wanted. They are a vehicle, not a gap. The stalk is still blinking. Cancel is a sentence. Taking it is a sideswipe.

options.text: Finish the change — they will make room, they are smaller
options.result: You take the left anyway. They are already in it. Steel on a fairing. They go down in the rain. Smaller is not a hole you get to occupy.

options.text: Cancel, hold your lane, let them show or pass, then take a swept gap
options.result: You kill the stalk and hold. They slide through the glass and go. The next gap is empty paint. You take it without writing a rider into the door.

options.text: Drift right first so they have more of the left
options.result: You drift right to be kind. A van is already in that space. You buy a sideswipe to avoid a sideswipe. The rider still has your old gap.

options.text: Tap the horn so they know to drop back
options.result: The horn on a wet morning. They flinch and stand it up. You both stop in live lanes. The stack behind you gets two new problems.

debrief: A motorcycle in the lane you wanted is already a vehicle in that lane. Cancel, hold, then take a gap you have swept. You saved a rider a door full of steel.

source.psdp_skill: Skill ten: city driving – part one
source.teaching_target: Treat a motorcycle as a full vehicle in the lane; do not change into a rider who is already there.

title: When Loud Is Right
hook: She wants the PA. The block is only tight.
scene: Ice at midday in a work pinch downtown. You have Encore. Ali is on the welded bench — an audience, which is the problem. A dump and a cone line have the block down to a crawl. The guarded red switch is under your hand. The four horns on the roof would clear this in a breath. They would also tell the whole Core you wanted a show. Loud is for a dying block. This one is only tight.
decision: The block is pinched and Ali is watching. Do you run the PA?

options.text: Hit the PA and clear the pinch — they will move if you make them
options.result: The horns take the block. Cones jump. The dump stands on it. Something at the far end of the pinch turns toward the sound. You bought a show and a new problem. Ali did not need the concert.

options.text: Hand Ali the wheel so you can stand up and shout the dump back
options.result: You invent a driver change in a live pinch. Ali has the suede wheel and no count-in. The dump does not care who is talking. You made passengers out of a crawl.

options.text: Leave the PA dead. Count a gap, take it, keep the horns for a block that is dying
options.result: The red switch stays off. You take a counted gap and slip the pinch. Ali stays on the bench. The horns stay a tool you did not spend on a show. The block stays only tight.

options.text: Tap a count-in on the horn so the dump knows you are serious
options.result: A rhythm on the horn is still a horn. The dump hears a dare. He holds. You wrote noise on ice and taught Ali that loud is how you ask.

debrief: Loud is right when a block is dying and the horns buy people a path. A tight pinch is not that. Yuna keeps the horns for a dying block.

title: Backing Into People
hook: Mid-reverse. A coat just stepped into the aisle.
scene: Heavy rain under flat gray overcast. You are at the wheel of the Menace, twisted looking back, nose-in in a marked perpendicular stall. Ordinary cars parked tight on both sides hide the aisle until your rear clears the bay. Reverse lamps are already lit. The Beetle is partway out, wheels cut, backing into the aisle. One dark coat has stepped into that aisle from behind a neighboring car — only partly visible. They are not looking at your lamps. Yield is the whole reverse, not a glance before you roll.
decision: You are mid-reverse out of the stall and someone has entered the aisle. How do you leave?

options.text: Reverse now — they will see the lamps and move
options.result: You come out on a guess. They do not see the lamps in the rain. The plow is the wrong end for this. You write a coat into a stall exit. The lot did not need that sound.

options.text: Honk the whole reverse so they know a car is coming
options.result: You back up shouting. They jump and scatter into the other aisle lane. A primer car has to lift. Sound got them off your paint and onto someone else's.

options.text: Wait until they pass, then creep out and stop if anyone new enters the aisle
options.result: You wait once and then commit. A third coat steps off the curb after you are already rolling. Waiting is not the same as checking the whole time you move.

options.text: Wait them out, check both ways, creep, and be ready to plant it the whole reverse
options.result: You let the coat clear. You look both ways. You creep. A second person appears and you plant it. They pass. You finish into an empty aisle. The stall stays a stall.

debrief: Angled and straight-in stalls back into a live aisle. People in that aisle own it until they are gone. Wait for them to clear, then creep.

title: Door Before You Step
hook: Parked parallel. The door wants the bike lane.
scene: Clear cold dawn, a downtown curb, you already nailed the parallel — plow in line, wheels straight, one foot from the curb. The engine dies. Marisol is a dark shape in the left door glass, closing fast in the bike lane you just boxed with a door that has not opened yet. The Dutch reach is the far hand, look, then the latch. Opening the near hand is how a bike becomes a story.

options.result: You reach across. The turn puts the glass in your face. Marisol is a whole bike, not a smear. You wait. She passes. The door opens on empty paint. She does not have to lift.

options.text: Wait until you cannot see her, then open fast and get it over with
options.result: Losing her in the glass is not a clear. She is in the blind stretch along the door. You open into a bike you decided was gone. The curb takes both of you.

title: Already In the Circle
hook: Look left. Yield to the ones already in.
scene: Wind at morning on a downtown Seattle roundabout — raised island, truck apron, two lanes circling left. You sit at the yield line. A primer SUV is already in the circle on your left, coming around the island. Another car holds the right circle lane toward the exit you want. Yield to traffic already in. Look left on entry. Do not change lanes inside. Signal when you leave.

options.text: Enter now and cut across both lanes to the exit you want
options.result: You take both lanes at once. The SUV is already in. The right-lane car is already in. You invent a third path through two that had the circle. Steel on a primer quarter. The lane you picked was the one you keep.

options.text: Look left, yield to the SUV already in, enter the gap, stay in your lane, signal when you leave
options.result: You look left. The SUV owns the circle until it doesn't. You take the gap. You stay in the lane you picked. Amber on before the exit. Nobody has to guess. The island stays an island.

options.text: Stop in the circle until the SUV goes all the way around again

options.result: You wave. They hesitate. The gap you had closes. The car behind you does not know why you died at a yield that already had a rule. Politeness invented a stall the circle does not use.

debrief: Yield to traffic already in the roundabout. Look left on entry. Stay in the lane you picked. Signal when you leave.

title: The Conversation
hook: She found the bus. She's been fine.
scene:
The Ledger is still parked. Window to window. Fog on the cage. Glasses on the cord. Clipboard on the thigh. He does not ask you a question.

She found the bus. She's been fine.

Kent lot. I read the collar. I kept her.

I was measuring whether you stay quiet. Whether you check. Whether I can trust you with something that cannot protect itself.

Same test as a load. Same as the pass. Same as the license. One standard.

First time I am saying that out loud.

She goes back because I decided. You did not ask. You did not score this.

I carried someone else's cat. Waited to see if you'd mention it.

You never did. I know why.

Take her.

options.text: Brake in the right and wave the left through so they go first
options.result: You plant the Menace to look kind. The right stack lights. Take-turns is one-for-one at the teeth, not a courtesy stop in a live lane.

debrief: Use both lanes until the closure, then take turns. The zipper is take-turns, not an early courtesy move.

title: Three Seconds Here Too
hook: The gap looks big. Count it anyway.
scene: Wind, midday, I-90 east, three lanes. You want the left to pass a slow box. A sedan is coming up that left, not yet beside you. The gap looks like highway space — long pavement, easy. At this speed a car covers that pavement before you finish the thought. The same three-second count you used on side streets is the count for a merge, a change, and an exit. If you cannot count it, it is not a gap.
decision: The left looks open. When is it yours?

options.text: Take it now — at highway speed a long opening is already enough
options.result: You go. The sedan is in your left door before the stalk finishes. A long-looking gap at this speed was one second. You spent his brakes.

options.text: Watch a mark on the pavement. If you can count three before you reach it, take the gap
options.result: You pick a stain. One. Two. Three. The sedan is still back. The gap is real. You take one lane and sit.

options.text: Wait until you cannot see the sedan at all, even far back
options.result: You wait for an empty highway. The left never empties. The slow box stays your number. Three seconds was the test, not a deserted road.

options.text: Count one and go — three is a city number, not a highway number
options.result: One second at this speed is a car length you do not have. He lifts. The count did not change because the pavement got faster.

debrief: Use a three-second count to merge, change lanes, or exit. If you cannot count it, it is not a gap. Take the gap only after you can count three.

title: Flashers on the Strip
hook: The car starts pulling hard right.
scene: The car starts pulling hard right. The shoulder here is narrow, there's a curve in the road behind you, the light is going, and nobody is in the other seat.
decision: The car is pulling hard right. What do you do?

options.text: Keep it straight, get well past the curve, then pull all the way right and stay inside
options.result: You hold it through the bend, then take the strip: all the way right, flashers on, belt still clipped. You stay a shape inside steel. The curve is behind you, not under you.

options.text: Stop right here before it gets worse
options.result: You plant it in the bend. The next lamps come around a curve and find a Beetle with no sightline. The strip past the curve was the pad. Here is just the wall and the through.

options.text: Get out and look at what happened
options.result: You unclip and step onto a live freeway shoulder the width of a plate. A look at a soft tire is not worth a body on the fog line. The next lamps have no time.

debrief: If you have to stop on a freeway, get well past any curve, pull as far right as you can, turn on your hazard lights, and stay inside the car with your seatbelt on.

title: Where the Blacktop Quits
hook: The pavement ends and the mountain gets a face.
scene: The county road gives up about four miles past the last mailbox, and what replaces it is gravel that somebody graded in the spring and nobody has touched since. You are alone. Gracie is in the carrier, latched, strapped, because the wheels are turning. For five acts the pass has been a gray smudge you could cover with a thumb. From here it has snow on it and weather sitting down on the ridge like something settling in, and you can see which notch the road goes through.
debrief: Gravel from here. The pass is close enough to read now.

title: Loose Under You
hook: The tires are turning on something that moves.
scene: Gravel, washboarded in the wheel tracks, the Menace loose under you in a way pavement never is. Nothing here is holding the way you are used to anymore.
decision: How do you drive a surface that will not hold?

options.text: Same as pavement — the tires are the same tires
options.result: You drive it like asphalt and the back end goes light at the first bend. Loose is loose regardless of what you are used to.

options.text: Slow down, no sudden steering, gentle on both pedals, six seconds back
options.result: You come off the number. The inputs get small. The gap you keep is twice what the street asked for and the car stays under you the whole way.

options.text: Speed up so the tires skim the top instead of digging in
options.result: You go faster on the theory that speed floats. The washboard starts steering for you.

options.text: Ride the brake so you are always ready to stop
options.result: A dragged brake on gravel is a locked wheel waiting. You gave up the one thing you had, which was rolling.

debrief: Gravel: slow down, steer and brake gently, and double your following distance.

title: The Pile at the Edge
hook: Somebody left a ridge of gravel along the shoulder.
scene: A windrow runs the right edge for the next half mile — loose gravel piled where the grader pushed it and never came back. It looks like shoulder. It is a rope laid along the road.
decision: The windrow is on your right. Where do you put the tires?

options.text: Left of it, in the graded track, and give it room
options.result: You stay in the part somebody meant you to drive on. The pile sits out there being a pile.

options.text: Straddle it so you are using the full width
options.result: One wheel in loose and one in packed, and the car starts arguing with itself about which way is straight.

options.text: Ride the far right so oncoming traffic has all the room it wants
options.result: You put the right side into the windrow to be generous. It takes the wheel out of your hands and points you at the ditch.

options.text: It's only gravel — drive normally
options.result: It is gravel that is six inches deep in a line. That is not the same gravel you are already on.

debrief: Watch for windrows — piled gravel at the road edge grabs a wheel.

title: Off the Edge
hook: The right wheels are off the road.
scene: The road narrows where the culvert went in and the shoulder is a four-inch drop of soft dirt, and you find it the way everyone finds it — not by deciding. The right side goes down and the car pulls hard toward the ditch and the wheel in your hands wants one thing, which is to come back up. Everything in your arms agrees with it.
decision: Two wheels are off the pavement. What do you do?

options.text: Turn back onto the road — get the wheels up before the ditch
options.result: You pull. The tire climbs the lip, catches, and the car comes across the road with more angle than you asked for. That is how this crash happens. Not the drop — the fix.

options.text: Don't turn. Off the gas, hold it straight, find a flat spot and come back when it's clear
options.result: You keep the wheel where it is, which is the hardest thing in the car. The Menace runs the dirt straight, slowing. Twenty yards on the shoulder comes back up level and you signal and steer on, and the whole thing ends up being nothing.

options.text: Brake hard before you lose more of it
options.result: You stand on it with two wheels on dirt and two on asphalt, and the two that grip swing the car around the two that don't.

options.text: Jerk it back
options.result: You do it before you decide to. The tire catches the lip and the car is across the centerline and you are a passenger for the part that matters.

debrief: If you run off the road: don't turn the wheel, ease off the gas, stay straight, and come back on where it's level. Arms VI-011.

title: Wide and Slow
hook: A grain truck, swinging out for a gate you cannot see.
scene: A truck ahead doing thirty with a load and a slow-moving triangle. It drifts left, which on a two-lane looks like an invitation. There is a field entrance somewhere on the right that you have no way of knowing about and he does.
decision: He's moved left and slowed. What do you do?

options.text: Take the gap on the right — he's making room
options.result: He swung wide for a right turn into the gate. You put the Menace where the trailer is going.

options.text: Stay back until you can see his mirrors and know where he's going
options.result: You hold. His signal comes on late, the trailer swings, and the gate appears. From back here it was obvious.

options.text: Pass on the left immediately, before he slows more
options.result: Blind crest coming and a farm truck beside you. You cannot finish it. The pass dies unfinished.

options.text: Sound the horn so he knows you're behind
options.result: You make noise on a country road. He already knew. The horn did not buy you information.

debrief: Farm equipment makes wide turns at unmarked entrances. Make sure the driver can see you before you pass.

title: Nobody's In Charge Here
hook: No stop, no yield, no paint. Somebody still has to go second.
scene: Two gravel roads cross at the section line. No sign in any direction, no signal, nothing painted. A dusty pickup is coming from your right at about the same speed you are, and it is arriving at about the same time.
decision: No signs, and you'll both arrive together. Who goes?

options.text: He's on your right — slow, look twice, let him through
options.result: You come off it, check both ways twice, and let him have it. He lifts a finger off the wheel.

options.text: You were there first — keep your speed
options.result: Uncontrolled means nobody has it by default. You arrived together and you both believed you were first.

options.text: Speed up and clear it before he gets there
options.result: You race a stranger through a blind crossing on the theory that whoever commits harder wins.

options.text: Stop dead in the middle and wave him on
options.result: You stop in the intersection, in dust, on gravel, and now nobody knows what either of you is doing.

debrief: At an uncontrolled intersection, slow down, check both ways twice, and yield to the vehicle on your right.

title: Five Easy Steps
hook: A circle with nobody in charge of it.
scene: A single-lane roundabout where the county road meets the state route, and a sedan is already inside it coming around toward your entry. You have never liked these. Yuna says they're the safest intersection anyone builds, which is easy to say on a radio.
decision: You're at the entry. A car is already in the circle.

options.text: Slow to about fifteen, yield to him, then take the gap behind
options.result: You come down to fifteen, look left, and let him have it. Then the gap opens and you go without stopping again.

options.text: Stop at the line and wait for the whole circle to clear
options.result: Nobody empties a roundabout. You stop, then stop again, and the three cars behind you inherit it.

options.text: Enter now — you're moving and he can adjust
options.result: He's already in. Traffic in the circle has it, and you just asked a stranger to brake for your entry.

options.text: Enter, then change lanes inside to reach your exit sooner
options.result: Single lane, and you came in planning to move around in there. There is nowhere left to sort it.

debrief: Slow down, look left, yield to traffic already in the roundabout, don't stop inside, and signal your exit.

title: Pick Your Lane Before the Circle
hook: Two lanes in. The decision is on the approach, not inside.
scene: Bigger roundabout at the highway junction, two lanes going in, arrows painted on the approach and a sign board before them. Your exit is the third one — effectively a left. The lane you're in decides whether you can take it.
decision: Two lanes, your exit is the far side. Where do you get in line?

options.text: Read the signs and arrows now, take the left lane, stay in it around
options.result: You read the board, take the left, hold your lane the whole way, signal, and leave. Decided before you entered.

options.text: Take the right lane and move left once you're inside
options.result: Changing lanes in a roundabout is how the side of your car meets somebody who was already there.

options.text: Take whichever lane is shorter and sort it out inside
options.result: You pick by queue length and end up on the wrong side of the circle at your exit.

options.text: Stay right and go around twice
options.result: You commit to a lap because you didn't read a sign. The circle takes another turn from you.

debrief: On a multi-lane roundabout, read the signs and arrows before you enter and stay in your lane all the way around.

title: Look for the Others
hook: A deer in the road, and it is not alone.
scene: Last light. A doe is standing in your lane, broadside, doing what they do, which is nothing. Ditch on the right, oncoming lane on the left, and your hands have already decided which one they like.
decision: She's in your lane. You can't stop in time.

options.text: Brake straight, stay in the lane, don't swerve
options.result: You brake hard and hold the wheel and hit nothing, or you hit her and keep the car. Either way you're still pointed down the road — and the second one comes out of the ditch three seconds later.

options.text: Swerve left into the oncoming lane
options.result: The worst crashes are people who missed an animal and found a truck. Oncoming finds you first.

options.text: Swerve right onto the shoulder
options.result: Soft shoulder, a ditch, and a Beetle rolling into it. The ditch takes the car the deer never needed.

options.text: Swerve
options.result: Your hands did it. That is the whole reason this card exists. The swerve was the decision.

debrief: Don't swerve for an animal — slow down, be prepared to stop, and look for more. Deer travel in groups.

title: Over the Top
hook: You can't see the other side of the hill.
scene: The road climbs to a crest and drops away, and beyond it a curve you can't see the far end of. Whatever is on the other side is already coming toward you.
decision: Blind crest, then a curve. How do you take it?

options.text: Slow before the crest, move right, look as far through as you can
options.result: You come off it early, hold right, and the far side turns out to have a tractor in the middle of the road with the sun behind it.

options.text: Keep your speed — you'll see it when you're over
options.result: Over the top at speed with a tractor at forty yards and nothing but reflex left.

options.result: You improve your sightline by putting the Menace in the oncoming lane on a blind hill.

options.text: Brake in the middle of the curve once you can see
options.result: Braking mid-bend on gravel is how the back end goes around. The curve owns the car now.

debrief: Slow down before a crest or a curve, move to the right, and watch for what's coming.

title: Same Culvert
hook: The road narrows where the culvert went in.
scene:
Ten miles on and here is the same kind of place — a narrowing, a four-inch lip, soft dirt below it. You know what it looks like now because you have already been down there once today, and the thing you remember is not the drop. It's your own arms wanting to pull.

Nothing happens. You hold the middle of the lane and go by it at thirty and it is the least eventful hundred feet of the afternoon, and that is the whole point. The one earlier cost you a fence post and a hubcap. This one cost nothing because you had already spent it.
debrief: Off the road: don't turn, stay straight, come back where it's level. You paid for that one already.

title: Crossbuck and Nothing Else
hook: No gates. No bells. No lights.
scene: A yellow round sign with an X on it, and then two hundred feet on, a white crossbuck and two rails through the gravel. That's the whole crossing. No arms, no bells, nothing that will tell you. The corn is high enough on the left that you cannot see up the line, and a train doing fifty is quieter than people expect until it isn't.
decision: An unmarked crossing, and you can't see up the line.

options.text: Slow, roll down the window, look both ways and listen, then cross
options.result: You come down to almost nothing, drop the glass, look left and right and left again, and hear nothing. Then you cross without stopping on the rails.

options.text: No gates means no active line — keep your speed
options.result: The gates are missing because nobody built any. The line is live. Absence of arms is not absence of trains.

options.text: Stop on the rails to get a better look both ways
options.result: You park the Menace on the one strip of ground you must never stop on. The rails are not a viewpoint.

options.text: Speed up to be across sooner
options.result: You take a blind crossing at speed on gravel. Less time exposed, no time to react.

debrief: At a crossing with no gates or lights: slow down, look both ways, listen, and be ready to stop.

title: The Clipboard, Again
hook: He's in the seat beside you with the log.
scene:
Deac in the passenger seat for the first time since Central, the metal clipboard on his knee and the same hand-ruled sheet he has been carrying since Kent. He is not talking. He says drive to the crossing and turn around, and then he says nothing for eleven miles while you do gravel and a crest and a roundabout, and the only sound is the pen.

At the end he turns the sheet around so you can see it, which he has never done, and there are hours in the left column and a line at the bottom with his initials on it.
decision: He's holding it out. What do you say?

options.text: Nothing — take it, read it, hand it back
options.result: You read your own hours. He takes it back and clips it down. "That's the state's form," he says. "I run it out of the book because there's nobody left to run it out of anything else. You passed it."

options.text: Ask which parts you got wrong
options.result: "You want the list, I'll give you the list." He does. It is short and it is not the point right now.

options.text: Ask if this means you can take the pass
options.result: "It means you can drive. What the mountain does about it is the mountain's business."

options.text: Tell him you were nervous
options.result: He looks at the sheet. "Everybody is. I wrote down what you did, not what you felt."

debrief: The state's knowledge and skills standards are the standard, whoever holds the clipboard.
